articles.title: 80 Israelis and Americans, including NY Democrat Brad Lander, detained in West Bank
articles.summary: U.S. Democratic congressional nominee Brad Lander was detained along with about 80 American and Israeli rabbis and activists by Israeli security forces as they helped Palestinian olive harvesters.
body: NAHALIN, West Bank — U.S. Democratic congressional nominee Brad Lander was detained along with about 80 American and Israeli rabbis and activists detained by Israeli security forces as they helped Palestinians harvest olives from their grove close to a settlement in the occupied West Bank.

Lander, the former New York City comptroller, later said on social media he has been released from Israeli military custody — he presumed because of his "public profile" — but several dozen others are still detained.

This is the largest mass detention of activists in the occupied West Bank in at least a decade, two Israeli lawyers who work on related cases told NPR. Rabbi Arik Ascherman, a longtime Israeli human rights proponent, called the detentions "unprecedented." This comes amid a spike in violence by Israeli settlers against Palestinian farmers in the West Bank.

The Israeli military said in a statement that harvesting in the area requires the farmers to submit requests to the authorities before the olive harvest season in order to coordinate "security of the area and maintain public order." The military said Palestinians in this area did not submit a request, so soldiers and police arrived and detained those present.
"Regarding reports of the detention of a congressional candidate, we note that he was released once the matter was brought to our attention," the Israeli military told NPR.

"We've been detained by the Israeli military for harvesting olives, and let's be clear: Occupation is a crime under international law," Lander said in a video he filmed from the bus the group was loaded onto to be taken to a police station. "Harvesting olives is not a crime under any law."

American rabbis from the U.S. organization T'ruah, the Israeli group Rabbis for Human Rights and other activists had joined Palestinian families in picking olives at their grove in Nahalin, close to the Israeli settlement of Beitar Illit.

Olive harvesting is an important time for Palestinians both culturally and economically. But it has become increasingly hard for Palestinians in the occupied West Bank to access their fields. Several Palestinians there told NPR they have been unable to harvest their olive trees there since the Hamas-led attack on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, saying it had become too dangerous in the face of rising settler attacks in the occupied West Bank.

The detentions come less than a week after American photojournalist Heidi Levine, working for The Washington Post was assaulted by Israeli settlers in the West Bank, the latest journalist to come under attack during the Palestinian olive harvest season. Democratic congressman Ro Khanna of California was also briefly detained by Israeli forces while visiting the West Bank in July.
On Wednesday, the group of Americans and Israelis joined the Palestinian farmers hoping their presence would help them harvest in peace. T'ruah said the action was called Protect the Harvest.

After roughly two hours, drones began circling overhead and Israeli security forces arrived and declared the area a closed military zone. They detained the Israeli and American activists and took them to the police station for questioning. The rabbinical human rights group T'ruah said a Palestinian family was also detained.

"Let us be clear about what happened here: Rather than protecting Palestinian farmers and ensuring their right to work their own land, the Israeli military forcibly removed those who came to provide a protective presence," T'ruah CEO Rabbi Jill Jacobs said in a statement. "This is an outrageous abuse of power, and part of a systematic, state-backed campaign of ethnic cleansing aimed at driving Palestinians from their land," she said.
Israeli authorities have rejected accusations of ethnic cleansing.
This is a developing news story, which may be updated.
Daniel Estrin reported from Tel Aviv, Israel, where Itay Stern also contributed reporting.

articles.title: DOJ's noncitizen voter list is unreliable, officials say. And, U.S. pollution rises
articles.summary: The Justice Department's "likely" noncitizen voter list in California is "unreliable," according to officials. And, the United Nations reports a major increase in U.S. climate pollution.
body: Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Los Angeles County election officials say that the Justice Department's list of 20,000 "likely" noncitizens registered to vote is "unreliable," based on their preliminary analysis. They also say some of the individuals on the list have indicated they were born in the U.S. and may be citizens. State and local officials disclosed these new details in court filings yesterday, in response to a federal lawsuit demanding that California investigate thousands of voters before their ballots are counted. The DOJ wants the state to segregate ballots associated with these individuals. California officials say the DOJ's request is unfeasible so close to the election and may violate federal and state election laws.

A new report from United Nations scientists says that countries are not doing enough to cut emissions that drive climate change, and the United States plays a significant role in climate pollution. The U.S. was the only major economy that saw an increase last year in planet-warming pollution. The report also found that, among G20 countries, the U.S. is tied with Russia for the highest per capita emissions. While China emits more total greenhouse gases annually than the U.S., China's population is more than four times that of the U.S. The rise in U.S. emissions was fueled by increased electricity demand and Trump administration policies that support burning fossil fuels.

Arrests for low-level crimes, including vagrancy and drug possession, increased in the U.S. from 2024 to 2025, according to a new analysis of federal data from the criminal justice and immigration reforms advocacy group FWD.us. The report also highlighted a 188% increase in immigration violations. This comes as violent crime rates, including homicides, dropped to historic lows. The report examined publicly available FBI and immigration arrest data and does not include details about whether charges were dropped or if people served any time in jail or prison. This data covers the first full year of Trump's second term, during which his administration emphasized a tough-on-crime approach. Zoë Towns, the executive director of FWD.us, told NPR ahead of the report's release that the rising trends signal a "really troubling return to some of the extreme law and order policies that defined the American criminal justice system during the '80s and '90s." Check out NPR's analysis.

President Trump's envoy Steve Witkoff is in St. Petersburg today to meet with Kremlin officials and explore potential solutions for ending Russia's war on Ukraine. Witkoff also met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy this week in Norway. Trump has accused Zelenskyy of obstructing a peace deal. The Ukrainian president says he is again seeking direct talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin.

The results of the 2026 midterm elections will shape the final two years of President Trump's second term and serve as a precursor to the 2028 general election. This month, Morning Edition is reporting from six states that could change the balance of power in Washington.

This week, Morning Edition's Steve Inskeep traveled to North Carolina and Georgia. Both states are among those Trump visited this week as he continues to campaign for Republicans vying to keep control of the Senate and House. Inskeep explored how the Trump administration's policies have affected public research in both states. Trump has eliminated hundreds of jobs from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, which is headquartered in Atlanta. Universities and research firms in North Carolina's Research Triangle lost millions of dollars in federal grants last year. Inskeep spoke with people affected by these changes. Listen to what they had to say.
Hear more from voters in both states:

The NPR App has all of NPR's election coverage in one place — from the biggest stories across the country, to the issues that matter close to home. Browse headlines, playlists, podcast episodes, videos and more, all on the 2026 Election tab.
Follow the reporting: Ohio and Michigan coverage airs Oct. 27. You can follow along on Morning Edition, NPR.org, in the NPR app and in this newsletter.
by Tommy Evans, NPR's editor in chief

To cover a transformation as vast as AI, one that raises deep questions about work, culture, the environment, cybersecurity, education and so much more, we've teamed up with veteran tech journalists Casey Newton and Kevin Roose to bring their flagship AI podcast, Machine Gods, to NPR's audiences. Starting today, the video-first program will be offered twice a week across NPR's platforms and provide front-row access to the people and issues shaping this new AI era.

The show will look into things like the ways AI could be applied to the medical field, potentially helping us discover new drugs and improve healthcare overall, as well as the questions that keep Casey and Kevin both up at night, like what happens when AI eventually builds and improves upon itself beyond what humans understand. With each episode, we'll make sure you get the news you need to know about AI — both the technology's capabilities and its very real risks — without buying into the industry's hype or treating catastrophe as an inevitability.

Machine Gods is the culmination of years of Casey and Kevin's reporting from the front lines of Silicon Valley. While it represents an ambitious new format for public media, its core ethos fits seamlessly with NPR's mission: to bring audiences trusted, independent journalism that inspires, engages, and keeps you informed so you can navigate the world with confidence.
You can see the first episode here.
Follow and subscribe to Machine Gods on the NPR app, NPR.org, or wherever you get your podcasts.
This newsletter was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.

articles.title: Russia releases imprisoned U.S. citizen Stephen Hubbard following Trump's request
articles.summary: The announcement of Hubbard's release came as talks got underway between Putin and White House envoy Steve Witkoff in Saint Petersburg focused on the latest U.S. efforts to end the war in Ukraine.
body: MOSCOW and KYIV - Russian President Vladimir Putin says he has freed an American, Stephen Hubbard, 74, from a Russian prison following a request from President Trump.

The announcement came as talks got underway between Putin and White House envoy Steve Witkoff in Russia's former imperial capital of Saint Petersburg focused on the latest U.S. efforts to end the war in Ukraine.

Hubbard, a former school teacher native to Michigan, was detained by Russian forces in eastern Ukraine in 2022 and later sentenced — after a closed trial in 2024 — to nearly seven years in prison, for allegedly serving as a mercenary in the Ukrainian army.
The U.S. formally designated him wrongfully detained under the Biden administration.
And yet his case was front and center as the Kremlin leader hosted Witkoff for a meeting at Saint Petersburg's ornate Constantine Palace intended to focus on a new U.S. peace plan for Ukraine.
In introductory remarks, Witkoff thanked Putin for arranging Hubbard's release — to which Putin confirmed the American was already at Saint Petersburg's Pulkovo airport waiting to depart Russia.
"You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian," said Witkoff. "You are a humanitarian also, sir."
Russian state media later issued footage of a smiling Hubbard shaking hands with Witkoff as the Kremlin's White House envoy, Kirill Dmitriev, looked on.
President Trump – who had signalled a deal was in the works in comments to journalists earlier in the week – celebrated the news.
"Welcome home Stephen, it's great to have you back," Trump wrote on Truth Social, adding the U.S. hadn't given "anything in return."

"There was no "swap" necessary for this release. This major return should have taken place long ago through the Biden Administration, which got nowhere in its negotiations with the Kremlin," Trump added.
In a statement, Hubbard's son, Father Joseph Coleman, also thanked President Trump – and President Putin – for securing his father's release.
"We have been gravely concerned for his safety and health since his 2022 detention," wrote Coleman in a statement.

Witkoff's comment calling Putin a humanitarian enraged Ukrainians, who see the Russian leader as the driving force behind Russia's full-scale war on Ukraine, the biggest, bloodiest and deadliest war in Europe since World War II.
The United Nations has verified more than 17,000 civilian deaths in Ukraine since the start of the Russian invasion in 2022.
Oleksandr Merezhko, who chairs the foreign affairs committee in Ukraine's parliament, called Witkoff's statement "a total disgrace for America, American diplomacy and even for President Trump."

"It's like calling Hitler a humanitarian in the middle of the Second World War," Merezhko told NPR in an interview. "Putin is commiting genocide against Ukrainians. And when Witkoff is calling him a humanitarian and salutes him, to me, it means he should be immediately removed, and he shouldn't represent the United States."

Hubbard's release comes as Trump has lifted some sanctions on Moscow, including an agreement to buy sanctioned Russian diesel fuel. That decision has angered Ukraine and its European allies who argue the move helps fund the Kremlin's war chest.
In televised comments to Witkoff, Putin announced the first tankers carrying 60,000 tons of Russian diesel would be departing for the U.S. in the next "2 or 3 days."
A Kremlin aide, Yuri Ushakov, later told journalists Putin had also agreed to restart 3-way peace negotiations with the U.S. and Ukraine, beginning in mid-November.

Prior to his arrival in Saint Petersburg, Witkoff met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, Norway's Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store and the Finnish President Alexander Stubb in Oslo. Zelenskyy requested the meeting amid a growing rift between Trump and Zelenskyy over Washington's sudden overtures to Moscow.

Trump, in particular, has railed at Zelenskyy for responding to Russia's daily – and deadly – missile attacks on Ukrainian cities with long-range drone strikes on Russian oil facilities. Kyiv says the strike campaign is an attempt to weaken Russia's ability to wage war on Ukraine, but Trump insists it is a key driver behind surging gas prices in the US ahead of midterm elections.
Economists say Trump's war in Iran — and Tehran's subsequent blockage of the Strait of Hormuz — has been the primary factor behind high global oil prices.

articles.title: Millions are struck off India's voter rolls in largest disenfranchisement in history
articles.summary: India is plunged into political crisis after 130 million names were struck off voter rolls during a massive revision.
body: NEW DELHI — Like many Indians, Kanchan has one name and lives in hardscrabble quarters. Her home is built of tin and a tarp, constructed under a flyover in the capital New Delhi. And like many on the margins, Kanchan was proud of her right to vote — a rare equalizer in unequal India.
"It's important, because it shows we are citizens," Kanchan said on a recent October day, sitting on a plastic chair as vehicles trundled overhead.

But a few weeks ago, Kanchan said about 500 adults were deleted from their voter roll in this community, which resides around a bridge. They found out through another resident who is allowed to examine the voter rolls as a representative of a political party.
They were among an estimated 130 million names that were deleted during a revision of voter rolls that began last year in June.

The number is an estimate by Yogendra Yadav, an elections specialist and prominent critic of Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). Nevertheless, the BJP has cited the figure as authoritative in its defense of the voter roll revision. The rolls once had listed 980 million names.

"The government is choosing the people that support them," Kanchan told NPR, accusing the BJP of engineering voter rolls to disenfranchise communities opposed to the party. That is a widespread belief among critics of the voter revision process, including a former chief election commissioner of India, SY Quraishi. "Normally voters choose the government, here the government was choosing the voters," said Quraishi, who served in that role from 2010 to 2012.

India's election commission, which is overseeing the voter revision, is ostensibly independent. But critics accuse chief commissioner Gyanesh Kumar of being partisan to Prime Minister Modi's party. And it is the party, not the commission, that has mounted a defense of the revision. In a video issued on the BJP's YouTube channel in early October, it said those approximately 130 million deleted names were of people who had died, had duplicate entries, had moved residences or were otherwise absent.
Kanchan said in her community, people were deleted on the basis they had relocated, even though an election official came to visit and she "made me sign and hand over the form to her."

And activists helping Indians get back on the voter roll say many others were deleted because they could not provide information that had never been demanded of voters before, like demonstrating that their parents or grandparents voted in elections more than two decades ago. Others were told to prove who they were after discrepancies appeared between how their names were spelled on voter rolls and how they were spelled on enumeration forms that were distributed to some, but not all, voters.

One notice was handed to Nasir Malik, a community activist in a New Delhi quarter called Mustafabad, who waved it around on a recent day. "This makes no sense," he told NPR. "If this was a problem, how did I vote in elections before this?"

Name spelling discrepancies are so common in India that experts said they were not regarded as a problem in previous voter roll revisions, as long as the local election official believed they were dealing with the same person.

In a downtown New Delhi café, a lawyer who has filed multiple petitions against the voter revision process said his country once took pride in ensuring that every eligible adult could vote. Now, the burden of proof was flipped onto citizens to prove who they were, triggering "the largest disenfranchisement exercise in human history," said the lawyer, Kaustubh Chaturvedi. "It's an unconscionable process. What you've really done is you've purged the right to the vote from almost all of those who need it most."

It is the largest disenfranchisement by numbers. By ratio, the Jim Crow laws led to higher percentages of people being disenfranchised in the United States, according to historian Carole Anderson, who has written extensively about voter suppression of Black communities.
For 27-year-old Kanchan, in the New Delhi community around the bridge, her right to vote wasn't just about voting.

She's raising her 6-year-old son alone after her husband, a food delivery driver, was killed in a road accident four years ago. She supplements her teaching income with a monthly government stipend equivalent to $25, and free monthly food staples of rice, wheat and sugar. She feared authorities would deny her those services by calling into question her citizenship, because she was struck off voter rolls. "They'll cut us off from everything slowly," she fretted.
Those fears were particularly triggered after government officials in some states ruled by the BJP vowed to strike people off assistance programs if they'd been deleted off voter rolls.

After an outcry over voter deletions in September, the election commission said it worked with "complete integrity." It said officers would help those deleted from voter rolls to be reinstated. Sunil Kumar, a senior election official in Kanchan's constituency of Chandi Chowk told NPR that his department was working to get Kanchan's community back onto voter lists.
Any help now has come too late for some disenfranchised Indians, like Malika, who only has one name.

In the working-class quarter of Mustafabad, Malika worried she'd now be accused of being an illegal migrant, because she was struck off voter rolls. Her concern stems from the claim by the powerful interior minister, Amit Shah, who first said the voter revision would be aimed at detecting, deleting and deporting infiltrators. And while authorities tried to quell protests against the voter revision deletions in October, Shah described those opposing the voter revision as protecting infiltrators. That is often a dog whistle in India for Muslims from neighboring Bangladesh.

Malika, who is Muslim, says her voter ID was one of the few ways she could prove who she was. She was born without a birth certificate, says she never went to school and that her parents died when she was young. "I had no elders," she said. "I pretty much raised myself."

She said she was struck off her old voter roll in Mustafabad after she moved two hours away — she couldn't afford the rent after her husband was killed in communal violence here six years ago. More than 40 people were killed, mostly Muslims, by Hindu mobs. Malika now commutes to Mustafabad each day where she works as a cleaner, making $80 a month, which she said barely feeds her three children.

She said no election officer ever visited her in her new digs to take down her details, which they were supposed to do so she could get back on the voter roll. Malika said she'd visited her local officer on a recent Friday, but she lost a day's work without resolving anything.

"These people, the government officials — they like to sit in their air-conditioned offices and they make certain rules," she said, referring to the voter revision process. "But they really need to come to the ground and see how it is," she said, "to work in the hot sun, to be poor like we are."

For now, she signals her identity through the plastic bangles on her arms, colored orange, white and green — the colors of the Indian flag. She smiled as she jangled them. "This is my India too," she said.

articles.title: Zelenskyy says early warning system for Russian missile attacks resumes
articles.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the change happened after talks with his American counterparts, including a phone call with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
body: KYIV, Ukraine — Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Tuesday that Kyiv is once again receiving early warnings from its partners about incoming Russian missiles following recent strikes that he said occurred without enough notice, leaving civilians vulnerable.

For at least a week, the Ukrainian leader has said that his country has not received early warnings about ballistic missiles aimed at the capital. Such intelligence, he said, saves lives by allowing the public to be alerted and giving military units time to try to intercept the missiles.
Zelenskyy said the change happened after talks with his American counterparts, including a phone call with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

"We are thankful that intelligence works now, and I'm speaking about early warning, which is very important for our people, for children, adults, civilians, because we can hear when ballistic is coming," Zelenskyy said on a visit to Norway. "So we are thankful to American side now that it works."

Speaking to reporters in India, Rubio acknowledged mutual frustration between the U.S. and Ukraine over intelligence sharing and weapons supplies but emphatically denied that the Trump administration has made any changes to previous policy on either issue.

In other developments, Russia unleashed another missile and drone blitz of civilian areas in Ukraine, killing at least nine people, officials said, as Zelenskyy sought more American and European help.

Zelenskyy was joined in Norway by U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff, who has tried without success to steer Russia and Ukraine toward a settlement to end the war. Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre and Finnish President Alexander Stubb also met with the Ukrainian president in Norway's capital.
Gahr Støre said Witkoff planned to fly to St. Petersburg on Wednesday to meet with Russian leaders, exchange ideas from the Oslo meeting and share proposals from European and American colleagues.
"Today was a good day for peace," Stubb said.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said Moscow is willing to listen to new U.S. proposals about Ukraine but doesn't expect any "miracle" from Washington.
At the White House, President Donald Trump stepped up the pressure on Zelenskyy to come to an agreement with Russia as relations between the two men have soured again.
"We want Zelenskyy to make a deal," Trump told reporters in the Oval Office. "We've given a lot to Ukraine. We've gotten absolutely nothing back except grief, death, tremendous monetary loss."
If that doesn't happen, "I think it's going to be a very bad thing."
The conversation with Rubio came after Zelenskyy told a bipartisan group of U.S. lawmakers Monday that he believes "some political decision has been made to slow down ... support for us."

Ukraine has nearly run out of American-made Patriot air-defense interceptors that it needs to stop Russian ballistic missiles, according to Zelenskyy, who has pleaded for Washington to send more. But he said the Pentagon is delaying the delivery of missiles that other countries have purchased for Ukraine.

The Ukrainian leader also said speed restrictions were still in place on his country's use of Starshield, the military-grade version of U.S. company SpaceX's satellite internet service Starlink, hampering battlefield operations.
Trump also has waived sanctions on Russia, a move that Zelenskyy slammed as helping Putin push on with Moscow's full-scale invasion, which will hit the five-year mark in February.
Zelenskyy said he had "a substantive conversation" with Rubio.
"I am grateful for his readiness to help and his clear position," Zelenskyy said on social media.
Rubio, who arrived Tuesday in India on an official trip, denied that the U.S. is withholding assistance from Ukraine.
"Nothing has changed," he told reporters.
The Patriot ammunition Ukraine needs is in short supply and is also required elsewhere in the world, Rubio said.
"There has not been some deliberate political directive to go out and harm Ukraine," he said.

European countries, worried about Russia's plans on the continent and viewing Ukraine as a bulwark against Moscow's ambitions, are trying to take up the slack of any falloff in U.S. supplies, but some key assets are American-made.

European countries and European Union institutions have allocated 237 billion euros ($266 billion) to support Ukraine, compared with 115 billion euros ($129 billion) from the U.S., according to Germany's Kiel Institute, which tracks assistance to Kyiv.

EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas on Tuesday questioned whether U.S. negotiators have been honest brokers in peace efforts. Ukrainian officials say the Trump administration has encouraged Kyiv to surrender land to Russia in return for peace.

"Although American negotiators have been trying to push Ukraine into surrender for … one and a half years now," Ukraine has not surrendered on Putin's terms "because Europe has been supporting Ukraine," Kallas said.
Four people were killed and 27 others wounded, including children, in Russian missile and drone attacks on the Kyiv region over the past day, regional police said.

Three were killed and six were wounded in the Obukhiv district, where warehouses were damaged, police said. In the Bucha district, one woman was killed and 21 people were wounded, eight of them children, while hundreds of buildings were damaged, according to police.

On Tuesday morning, three people were killed and four injured when two vehicles caught fire in a Russian attack on the Kyiv-Odesa highway, Ukraine's State Emergency Service said. The dead included the driver of a shuttle bus that was hit. The bus transports people from Kyiv to the National Military Memorial Cemetery.
Two more people were killed in a Russian attack Tuesday on warehouses on the outskirts of Dnipro in central Ukraine, authorities said.
National grid operator Ukrenergo reported power outages in 12 regions of Ukraine following the Russian attacks.

The Russian Defense Ministry said in a statement that its forces carried out drone strikes on logistics centers, port infrastructure and three cargo ships in the port of Reni in the Odesa region. It said that another bulk carrier was hit at sea on its way to Odesa.
Meanwhile, air defenses intercepted 136 Ukrainian drones over multiple Russian regions overnight, the ministry said.

articles.title: France announces nightly curfews 'for as long as necessary' in Paris and other cities
articles.summary: Fresh curfews were being imposed across the city centers of Paris and Lyon on Tuesday after the first quiet night since France's most destructive rioting in years.
body: PARIS — Fresh curfews were being imposed across the city centers of Paris and Lyon on Tuesday after the first quiet night since France's most destructive rioting in years, as Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said a "massive" security operation was planned for new protests Saturday.

Paris police said the curfew in two designated zones — around Place de la République and the Les Halles shopping district — had restored "public peace" overnight and would remain in place "for as long as necessary." The curfew zones leave out other areas hit on Saturday, including the Champs-Elysées and the area around the Saint-Lazare train station and parts of the Rue de Turbigo in central Paris, where protesters set up barricades and lit fires.
In Lyon, one of France's largest cities, authorities also renewed a curfew in the city center from 9 p.m. to 6 a.m., saying no disturbances had been recorded overnight.
Marseille, France's second-largest city, imposed a curfew for unaccompanied minors starting Tuesday night. Lecornu said the targeted curfews "helped keep last night calm."
Student unions and groups from the " yellow vest " movement, whose protests over fuel prices shook France in 2018 and 2019, have called for another day of protests Saturday.

Soldiers from Sentinelle, the anti-terrorism operation that has patrolled French cities since the 2015 Islamic State group attacks, will take over guarding sensitive sites to free up more police officers and gendarmes for crowd control, Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez told lawmakers Tuesday.
"The deployment (of police forces) for next Saturday will be massive," Lecornu told the National Assembly, France's lower house of parliament, without giving figures.

Police on Tuesday arrested a suspect in the arson attack that charred the historic city hall in Limoges, in central France, Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin said, adding that the person was being held in police custody and may not have acted alone.

French media reported that the suspect was close to radical environmentalist movements and was on a watchlist of people considered potential threats to national security. Darmanin declined to comment on the suspect's profile, but said far-left groups appeared to have organized to attack symbols of the state throughout France.

Footage of the 143-year-old building in flames, its bell tower collapsing, spread widely online over the weekend. U.S. Vice President JD Vance shared it on X, blaming the unrest on immigration and writing, "I pray that France, a beautiful country of amazing people, will stop this madness before more of its landmarks burn." President Donald Trump, who also relayed the video, said migrants had "taken over France."

French officials have instead blamed the violence on far-left groups and opportunistic looters. At least 2,400 people were arrested after rioters in cities across France on Saturday clashed with police, set cars on fire and stormed public buildings, during nationwide protests against rising living costs and poor conditions in schools.
On Sunday evening, small groups set fire to trash bins, bicycles and other objects in the streets and looted businesses in Paris, Lyon, Marseille and other cities.

In Paris on Monday night, a police helicopter circled over Place de la République overnight, a central point in the weekend clashes, sweeping the square with a searchlight to check that the curfew was being respected.

Early Tuesday morning, workers used a crane to remove a giant fluorescent yellow vest draped over the statue at the center of the square, then used pressure washers to blast graffiti off the monument.

Louise Belanger, a volunteer who came to help with the cleanup, said she still could not apprehend the level of violence. "Normally when you are 20 you should be optimistic, you should be starting to build something (...) If you are only anger and violence, what are you going to do? This is sad for everybody in society," she said.

Speaking in Lille, northern France, Darmanin said 149 people had been jailed nationwide as of Tuesday at noon. According to the Justice Ministry, of the roughly 2,400 people arrested since Saturday, more than 800 have been sent before prosecutors, most of whom were either put on trial immediately or ordered to appear at a later hearing.
In Paris alone, about 300 people have been sent before prosecutors following the Oct. 17 protests, the city prosecutor's office said in a statement.

Darmanin said he had asked prosecutors to appeal any sentence they considered too lenient. "People with no criminal record ending up in prison for property crimes is extremely rare, if not unheard of," he said, arguing that the French justice system will be "extremely firm."
In Lille, he said, three men aged 20 to 25 with no criminal record were each sentenced to 10 months in prison and jailed immediately for looting a video game store in the city's old town.
The National Assembly is launching an inquiry into the Oct. 17 violence and the authorities' policing strategy, its speaker, Yaël Braun-Pivet, said, with findings expected "by the end of the year."
Protests continued Tuesday on a smaller scale. Some 400 people, mostly high school and university students, marched in the western city of Rennes, and about 750 in Lyon, under pouring rain.

articles.title: Nigeria confirms an Ebola case in Abuja as a woman arriving from Uganda tests positive
articles.summary: Nigeria is the latest country to report an Ebola case as the outbreak spreads across the region. Kenya confirmed its first case earlier this month and has since recorded nine infections.
body: LAGOS, Nigeria — Nigeria confirmed an Ebola case in its capital, Abuja, on Tuesday after a woman who arrived from Uganda tested positive for the virus, the Health Ministry said.
The woman began showing symptoms on Oct. 7 and was admitted to a private hospital in Abuja on Oct. 11, where she was later diagnosed with Ebola.

Health Minister Muhammad Pate said authorities had begun tracing 44 people identified as contacts of the patient. "We are doing everything possible to contain this case by tracing all the contacts the individual may have had," he said.
Uganda had previously reported Ebola cases but it later declared itself free of the virus.
Nigeria is the latest country to report an Ebola case as the latest outbreak spreads across the region. Kenya confirmed its first case earlier this month and has since recorded nine infections.
Dr. Jean Kaseya, director general of the Africa Centers for Disease Control, said on X that "we are facing an extremely serious threat," with a fatality rate of nearly 50% of cases.
"This Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak has already become the most geographically extensive in history, affecting several countries spread across three regions of Africa," he said.

The Nigeria Centre for Disease Control said two weeks ago it was stepping up surveillance following the detection of Ebola in Kenya and strengthening the country's preparedness for a potential outbreak.

"These efforts have focused on early detection, isolation and referral, laboratory diagnosis, infection prevention and control, contact tracing, risk communication and protection of health care workers," the agency said.
Nigeria established an Ebola task force in June following the outbreak in Congo in mid-May.

"We do not want a repeat of what happened during the last outbreak when a carrier entered the country, and everyone was scrambling to respond," Femi Gbajabiamila, chief of staff to President Bola Tinubu, said when the task force was announced. "We have covered a lot of ground and established structures to address any potential threat."

The spread of Ebola beyond Congo has heightened longstanding fears among health authorities about the rapid transmission of the rare Bundibugyo virus, which has infected more than 9,000 people and killed more than 4,300 people.

The latest outbreak is the fastest-spreading Ebola outbreak on record and is on track to exceed the deadliest on record, West Africa's regional outbreak between 2014 and 2016, which killed 11,000 people, WHO has said. Nigeria was one of the countries affected, recording 20 cases before it was declared over in the country after three months.

articles.title: Russia frees US citizen Stephen Hubbard, state media reports
articles.summary: Stephen Hubbard has been taken to Pulkovo Airport, Putin said during talks with US envoy Steve Witkoff.
body: President Vladimir Putin says Russia has agreed to release an American citizen who was jailed for allegedly fighting on behalf of Ukraine, state media report.
Stephen Hubbard has been taken to Pulkovo Airport, Putin said during talks with US envoy Steve Witkoff in St Petersburg.
Hubbard, originally from Michigan, was 72 when he was sentenced to almost seven years in a penal colony in 2024.
Prosecutors said was serving in a defence unit based in the eastern city of Izyum when he was captured by Russian forces two years prior.

articles.title: Macron accuses foreign leaders of exploiting French riots
articles.summary: The comment is an apparent swipe at Benjamin Netanyahu and Donald Trump, who both face elections in coming weeks.
body: Violence raged in Marseille along with other French cities
French President Emmanuel Macron has accused foreign leaders of exploiting the riots which erupted across the country on Saturday for electoral purposes.
Without naming them, he said they were campaigning for forthcoming elections "at France's expense" with their comments on the violence, which erupted on the fringe of cost-of-living protests.
Speaking on a visit to the Middle East, he referred to them as "leaders who are in campaign mode, whether here in the region or on the other side of the Atlantic".
It was an apparent swipe at Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who faces parliamentary elections next week, and US President Donald Trump, for whom mid-term polls fall next month.
Macron said the unnamed leaders had been influenced by fake videos generated by AI about the riots.
Nearly 150 people have been jailed and more than 800 brought before the courts since the riots which gripped Paris and other cities including Lyon, Marseille and Nice.
Video of running battles between masked rioters and police, as well as property being destroyed and stores being looted, spread across social media.
The government admitted the police had "lost control" during the violence, which came after weeks of protests by students over conditions in high schools.
Macron vowed afterwards that the authorities would be "uncompromising" towards "agitators from ultra-left fringe groups", which he blamed for much of the trouble.
Clean up begins after French riots but police remain
Suspect arrested after historic town hall set alight - French media
Katya Adler: France divided over who to blame for riots and what to learn from them
In pictures: French landmarks damaged and destroyed by violent protesters
Katya Adler: France's government under pressure after weekend of widespread violence

Speaking in the Qatari capital Doha, the French president said: "For me, there is no visible foreign interference in the events that took place. On the other hand, there was foreign manipulation of information afterwards, yes, and that gave rise to unacceptable and stupid comments from many people, including foreign leaders...
"We had people claiming that we had been invaded by hordes of migrants and Islamists, which is completely false."
On Tuesday, Netanyahu said in an interview for Israel's i24 channel, external that France, which has Western Europe's largest Muslim minority, had been hit by an "invasion of extremist Islam".
He said he had told Macron after the Hamas attack on Israel on 7 October 2023: "If we do not eliminate them here, you will have them in Paris." "That is exactly what is happening," he added.
Also on Tuesday, Trump blamed the riots on mass immigration to France.

"When I look at France, when you look at Italy, when you look at all the turmoil and the hatred, that's not about school," he said. "That's about people coming into the countries that hate the country."
"Close your borders and take control before it is too late!" he said in remarks directed at Macron.
Israel's far right find fertile ground among first-time voters
Analysis: Trump's global headaches worsen weeks before crucial elections
Pink Panther rioting in France is actually AI

According to a report in the UK's Financial Times newspaper, external, EU regulators are examining possible foreign online interference and disinformation campaigns around the French riots and similar recent outbursts of unrest in EU states.

It quotes unnamed security officials as saying that pro-Russian and far-right social media accounts linked to previous disinformation campaigns have spread violent videos in an attempt to sow more chaos.
Iran and Algeria are also suspected of being behind some of the messaging, the paper adds.

David Colon, a researcher at France's Sciences Po university who specialises in disinformation, was quoted as saying that "pro-Kremlin influencers" linked to the Russian campaign Storm-1516 had "amplified the events and spread a number of false narratives".

France is one of Ukraine's most vociferous military supporters in its ongoing war with Russia, while Algeria is a former French colony with bitter memories of its war to achieve independence in 1962, and French relations with Iran have been strained by its war with the US and Israel this year.
BBC Verify has reviewed more than 15 examples of fake news videos on social media which researchers at the US-based dTeam say are the work of a Russian disinformation operation known as Matryoshka.
The videos feature near-identical branding to real news outlets in France, including Le Monde, Euronews and France 24.
The individual impact and reach of videos made by Matryoshka appear to be limited, but experts have said the focus on amplifying unrest is consistent with known Russian disinformation tactics.

Separately, BBC Verify has traced one of the most viral AI-generated images circulating on social media, which supposedly shows an elderly couple being robbed and left in their underwear in Paris, to an obscure website.
The director of Infos-Israel.News, Sabrina Hania, told the BBC her team had created the image - which was published on 17 October - using ChatGPT without using a reference image.

It was posted shortly after a television journalist reported on the alleged incident, citing "police information". The claim remains unconfirmed, with French media reporting that prosecutors have no information supporting it having happened.
While the original image was labelled as "Made with AI" on X and "AI content" on Instagram, it was later shared on X without any disclaimer in a post which attracted more than six million views.
Hania said she regretted that the image had been taken out of context and had misled so many people, blaming those who reshared it without identifying it as AI-generated.

articles.title: Australian MP loses both legs after alleged car attack, husband says
articles.summary: Her alleged attacker, 43-year-old Brendan Nugent, faces multiple charges and appeared in court for the first time on Wednesday.
body: Watch: 'Her heart and her mind are in good shape', husband of Helen Haines says
Helen Haines, the Australian MP who was hit by a car in what authorities say was a deliberate attack, has lost both her legs, her husband has confirmed.
Phil Haines said the"horrendous incident" caused his wife significant injuries but "her heart and her mind are in good shape". He added that the "good news in all this is that she's alive".
The alleged attacker, 43-year-old Brendan Nugent, faces multiple charges and appeared in court for the first time on Wednesday.

Nugent was arrested moments after he allegedly drove his Toyota LandCruiser into the independent MP outside her electorate office in the regional town of Wangaratta, about 240km (150miles) northeast of Melbourne.
Haines' "road to recovery will be long and difficult, but we know she is a fighter," her husband said at a press conference in Melbourne where she is being treated.
"She is a determined person who will do her best, with our support and love, to recover. And that is what we hope for."

He thanked hospital staff and people, both in Australia and internationally, who have shown their concern for Haines, and urged those who want to show their support to donate to the Save the Children fund.
"Please keep sending Helen your love," he added.

Earlier on Wednesday, Nugent appeared at the local court to face three charges: dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury, and causing harm to a Commonwealth public official. Police said more charges may be laid, including attempted murder.
Nugent - a local from the nearby town of Tarrawingee and known as an environmental campaigner - remained silent and emotionless during his brief court appearance.
He did not apply for bail and is due back in court in February. Court documents show he was also charged with cultivating and possessing cannabis.
In court, Nugent's lawyer said that his client had "mental health concerns" but did not give any further detail.
The court also heard that Nugent has a rare neurological condition - idiopathic transverse myelitis - caused by inflammation of the spinal cord.
Victoria Police said its investigation, with support from the Australian Federal Police (AFP), remains ongoing and a motive is yet to be established.
"His motivation for this - what we allege is a deliberate attack - is very much a centrepiece of the investigation," said Victoria Police Commissioner Mike Bush.
"Our people will continue to explore every element, angle and avenue to work that out. It's something that, when we work towards it, discover it, we will present in court."
Phil and Helen Haines have been married for nearly 40 years - next month is their anniversary
Nugent was not on the radar of police and there was no intelligence of any threat to Haines before the incident, police said.
Investigators are also looking into whether drug use or medication played a part in the incident and if there was any personal connection between Nugent and Haines.

Nugent's family earlier put out a statement saying they were long-time friends with Haines, who is the independent MP for the regional seat of Indi in Victoria. They described the apparent attack as "devastating and unfathomable".
The incident occurred on Monday afternoon at around 15.35, local time. Moments after the car hit Haines, bystanders pulled Nugent out of the vehicle and detained him.
Jacob and Jackie Evans were among the first on the scene, and said Haines was grateful to them for coming to her aid as she lay severely injured.
"Thank you, you lovely people," is what Haines said to them, according to the Herald Sun.
"She was thanking us, it was incredible," Jackie told Nine's Today programme.
Jacob used a tourniquet he had in a medical kit in his car to help stem the bleeding from one of Haines's legs.
Haines underwent surgery after the incident and lost one of her legs. As of Wednesday morning she has also lost the other leg, her husband Phil told reporters.
The community in Wangaratta, as well as the wider political community, are in shock over the incident in a country where political violence is rare.
Leaders from across the political spectrum have paid tribute to Haines, who was first elected in 2019 and is well regarded by her peers.
Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said he had spoken to Haines's husband several times since the incident.
In an interview with the national broadcaster ABC, Albanese said threats to female politicians were marked by a "different form of vilification and aggression" such as threats of rape.
There has also been a recent growing trend of threats against "high office holders", with almost one person a week being charged for such offences, police said.
Monday's incident has sparked debate over the level of security for MPs.
Federal police said that individual protection for every one of the country's 226 federal MPs would require "incredible" levels of staffing.
Instead, police assess the need for close personal protection based on a person's role and the threat environment around them, police said.
Australia's Governor-General Sam Mostyn, who spoke at the same press conference as Haines' husband, said this was "a moment for us to pause, and to choose to be better".
"We should do what I imagine Helen would be doing if she was not the victim of this terrible attack - reaching out to those who are terribly distressed by what has happened," she says.
"Most importantly, that we learn or re-learn to exercise our muscle of decency."

articles.title: Elon Musk says Tesla-SpaceX merger being considered
articles.summary: Musk says special committees within both companies have been formed to look at a possible mega-merger.
body: Elon Musk is the top executive of both Tesla and SpaceX
Elon Musk has said he likes the idea of a merger of Tesla and SpaceX, two of his most notable companies, and it is under active consideration.
"Do I think it would be a good idea? Yes," Musk said during a call with financial analysts over the quarterly business results of SpaceX on Tuesday.
While Musk noted the certainty of such a merger should not be assumed, and it would need shareholders' support, he said special committees within both companies have been formed to examine the move.

"The special committees have not reached agreement on terms of any transaction and there's no guarantee that they will," Musk added. "But I do think there is a lot of merit to merging and a lot to be gained."
With Tesla valued roughly $1.5 trillion and SpaceX valued at $2 trillion, a combination of the two companies would mark one of the largest mergers in history.
Shares of SpaceX rose 8% in after hours trading.
The company, which builds space rockets and Starlink internet satellites, is now expanding into offering cloud compute capacity for other tech companies, like Anthropic and Google.
That line of business has become the most profitable part of SpaceX, bringing in $7.5bn according to the latest quarterly results. Starlink also tallied revenue of $5.2bn.
SpaceX as a whole, however, is not profitable and has lost $1.1bn so far this year.
Shares of Tesla, which reports its own quarterly results on Wednesday, rose 2% after being down slightly for weeks.

Over the last year, Musk has taken to bringing more of his various companies under fewer banners. Before it went public earlier this year, SpaceX acquired xAI and X, the platform formerly known as Twitter, both of which Musk owned.

The recent launch of Terafab, a combined effort to manufacture computer chips between Tesla and SpaceX, was another signal that Musk sees his companies as potentially more effective when working together.
Musk said on Tuesday a full merger between the two companies would make sense for the work each is doing around chips, artificial intelligence, software and more.
Musk, who became the world's first paper trillionaire after the SpaceX stock market debut earlier this year, said he is not included in either of the special committees considering the mega-merger.
He described himself as a "conflicted party" as the chief executive of Tesla and of SpaceX.
Even commenting on the possibility of a merger between the two companies, Musk compared to "tap dancing through a minefield".
He added a merger would ultimately be decided by shareholders. At least 50% of Tesla's shareholders would need to approve the merger, which Musk described as "quite a high hurdle to achieve".
Shareholders have supported Musk's desires before. Last year, a majority of investors in Tesla approved a compensation package for Musk valued around $1 trillion.
While Tesla is known as an electric car company, Musk has lately been shifting resources there to work around robotics.
SpaceX, with its growing focus on AI infrastructure, quickly outstripped Tesla on the stock market in terms of value when it made its stock market debut.

articles.title: Pakistan arrests man wanted by US over $126m postage fraud case
articles.summary: Faheem Akram allegedly sold more than 5 million fake postage labels for a fixed price of $2 a piece.
body: Pakistan's cybercrime agency has arrested a man accused of running a counterfeit operation that caused $126 million (£94m) in losses to the US Postal service.
Faheem Akram is accused of having sold fake stamps via a fraudulent website in the US since 2023.

He was indicted by a federal grand jury in Florida last month for selling more than five million counterfeit shipping labels to thousands of US customers over the years. Authorities have now shut down the website.
Earlier this month, the US Postal Inspection Service offered a reward of up to $100,000 for information leading to his arrest.
According to the US Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Florida, the 33-year-old from Khanewal, Pakistan, operated LabelsBank.com.
US prosecutors alleged that he sold counterfeit US postage at a fixed rate regardless of a package's weight, size or destination.

The counterfeit labels, usually sold at $2 each, allegedly allowed customers to ship packages at rates far below legitimate prices, resulting in substantial lost revenue and shipping costs to the Postal Service.
An investigation found that more than 5,200 individuals purchased more than 5.1 million counterfeit shipping labels, the office said in a press release.

Akram is charged with one count of conspiracy to defraud the United States and to make and sell counterfeit postage stamps, five counts of making and selling counterfeit postage stamp labels, and four counts of wire fraud.
If convicted, he faces a maximum penalty of five years in prison on the conspiracy and counterfeit postage counts, and 20 years in prison on each wire fraud count, the office said.

articles.title: Gambia to pay victims of Yahya Jammeh's rule from proceeds of his seized US mansion
articles.summary: The Gambia has confirmed receiving $2.5m from the sale of the house in Maryland.
body: Jammeh ruled The Gambia for more than 20 years
The Gambia will use funds received from the US from the forfeiture of long-time ruler Yahya Jammeh's property to pay victims of his rule, authorities have said.
The Gambia's Reparations Commission said it received $2.5m (£1.86m) from the sale of a mansion in Maryland owned by former leader of the West African nation.
The US had in 2022 secured the right to sell the property on grounds that it was acquired through "criminal proceeds and misappropriated Gambian public funds".
Jammeh ruled The Gambia for more than 20 years after taking over in a coup in 1994 - a time marked by allegations of human rights abuses forced disappearances and extrajudicial killings.
How US mansion of Gambia's ex-president was seized
Profile: Former Gambian President Yahya Jammeh
On Tuesday, the Gambia Reparations Commission said it was "pleased to inform victims, survivors and the public that it has received a total of $2,573,414.10" from the sale of Jammeh's property.
It said it was committed to ensuring the funds were managed responsibly and transparently, "with due regard to the rights and needs of victims and survivors".
Jammeh lost to Adama Barrow in the election of 2016, first accepting defeat and then rejecting the results.
He eventually stepped down in 2017 amid intense regional and international pressure.
Troops from several West African nations, including Senegal, had been deployed to The Gambia, threatening to drive Jammeh out of office.
In the end he agreed to step down and went into exile Equatorial Guinea.
A national commission then discovered that the former president had 281 properties in The Gambia, as well as the one in the US and one in Morocco, and controlled more than 100 bank accounts.
There was no way that he could have afforded this on his salary and it concluded that he had misappropriated more than $300m.
Jammeh is accused of presiding over the murder of political opponents, disappearances, rape and torture.
A commission of inquiry found that widespread abuses had resulted in the death of "240-250 Gambians and non-Gambians at the hands of the state or its agents".

articles.title: Family of prison officer killed by IRA receives state apology
articles.summary: Brian Stack was crossing a street in Dublin in 1983 when he was shot in the back of the neck and died 18 months later.
body: Brian Stack was shot in the back of the neck as he left a boxing match in 1983
The family of a senior Irish prison officer murdered by the IRA has received a state apology on Wednesday for failings in investigations into his killing.
Brian Stack, a father of three, was crossing a street in Dublin, after leaving a boxing match in 1983, when he was shot in the back of the neck.
Stack, who was the chief prison officer at the high-security Portlaoise Prison, was left paralysed and died 18 months later, aged 49.
There were three separate garda (Irish police) investigations into Stack's death, but no-one was brought to justice for his killing.
The Taoiseach (Irish Prime Minister) Micheál Martin offered an apology on behalf of the state during a sitting of the Dáil (Irish parliament).
Stack's wife Sheila and her sons Austin, Kieran and Oliver were in the chamber for the apology.
Martin said the Provisional IRA is "still in the possession of all the facts" on this case.
Speaking to BBC Radio Ulster's Good Morning Ulster programme Brian Stack's son, Austin Stack, said the apology "means an awful lot to us".
"It's a great sense of comfort, to particularly my mother and to myself and my two brothers, because the state is officially owning up to the errors and the missions that happened," he said.
He went on to say that the serious crime review team looked into the first investigation and "they found 194 errors and omissions".
"So I have, and my family have, met with several ministers for justice down through the years and we have a requested sight of that report.
"And every time we've requested it, we've been told that it's an internally valid document and that we cannot see it."
Austin Stack said that Wednesday would be a very emotional day for his family.
"My dad was doing a very difficult job at a very difficult time in our history," he said.
"He was awarded the Irish Prison Service's highest bravery award for that work that he was doing. And this is further vindication of him and his good name."
Prior to the Dáil proceedings, the Stack family held a private meeting at government buildings with the taoiseach and Minister for Justice Jim O'Callaghan.
Taoiseach Micheál Martin formally apologised to the Stack family
In 2007 the Garda Commissioner directed a review of the case by the Garda Serious Crime Review Team. Over 200 recommendations were made relating to the cases.
This review led to "serious failings" being found as well as "the shortcomings in the management" of the earlier Garda investigation.

These failures, listed by Martin in the Dáil, are: failure to keep a map made of the crime scene, a failure to keep a motorbike helmet found near the crime scene and linked to the crime, a failure to keep custody of material exhibits, including various fingerprints, samples and debris gathered during the investigation.

The taoiseach also said there was a failure to document some potentially important aspects of the original investigation, including whether Brian's colleagues at Portlaoise Prison were interviewed and whether prisoners at the prison were interviewed.
There was also a failure to interview the Stack family and to interview Brian's wider group of friends.
"It is plainly and utterly unacceptable that material that was potentially of evidential value to the investigation can no longer be located by An Garda Síochána.
"It is admitted by An Garda Síochána that these are serious matters that had an impact on the investigation," Martin said.
He formally apologised to the Stack family for these failings.
NI secretary Sir Chris Bryant was asked about the matter in the House of Commons
Speaking in the Commons during Northern Ireland questions on Wednesday, Secretary of State Sir Chris Bryant said he "warmly welcomed" the apology.

Asked about the matter by Democratic Unionist Party leader Gavin Robinson, Sir Chris said Dublin doing so was "entirely right and proper" and went to the heart of discussions MPs had been having this week as they debated the UK government's Troubles legacy bill.
He added that it was "incumbent on all of us to make fulsome and not mealy-mouthed apologies".
The IRA admitted killing Stack in 2013 after his family mounted a long campaign to secure the admission, and met Sinn Féin's Gerry Adams and a former IRA commander.
Adams, at that time, expressed his "regret" to the Stack family over the killing.
A Sinn Féin spokesperson said that "in a 2013 statement, a former IRA leader acknowledged that IRA volunteers were responsible for Brian Stack's killing".

"The statement said the shooting had not been authorised by the IRA leadership, accepted IRA responsibility for his death, said it should not have happened and expressed sorrow for the pain and hurt suffered by the family."

The spokesperson added: "As republicans, we acknowledge the hurt caused by republican actions. That suffering cannot be disowned. We are sorry for all the lives lost during the period of conflict on this island, without exception."
Irish foreign affairs minister Helen McEntee said the Provisional IRA "are responsible"
Irish foreign affairs minister Helen McEntee also spoke during the State apology, she said: "The State failed you during their investigation into Brian's killing."
She said Brian was "targeted" by the Provisional IRA and said "they are responsible".

"To Sheila and to all of the Stack family, we are deeply sorry for all that you have endured, for the failures of the investigation and the additional suffering they have caused you, we are deeply sorry. I hope today's formal apology brings some measure of peace and comfort."
Donegal Sinn Féin TD (member of Irish parliament) Pearse Doherty said the Stack's family "long search for answers deserves respect".
"No apology can restore Brian Stack's life or return the years spent seeking answers but it can recognise the wrong done."
He said the failures of the garda investigation "compounded" the suffering of the Stack family.
In 2019, the family received an apology from then garda commissioner Drew Harris in relation to the handling of the investigation into the murder.
In 2023, gardaí told the family that the file on the case - which was with the DPP (Director of Public Prosecutions) - was being sent back to police for further investigation.
Stack was the only prisoner officer in the state killed by violence related to the Troubles in Northern Ireland.

articles.title: Nigeria confirms Ebola case linked to East Africa
articles.summary: The female patient, who sources have told the BBC is not Nigerian, is in isolation and in an Abuja hospital.
body: Medics across Africa, including these nurses pictured during a training drill in Kenya, have been on high alert since May
Nigeria has recorded a case of Ebola in a female patient who travelled from Uganda in East Africa to Abuja, capital of the West African state.
Health Minister Muhammad Ali Pate said the diagnosis had been confirmed by laboratory tests.
The patient, who health sources have told the BBC is not Nigerian and is the wife of a diplomat, is in isolation and receiving medical care after being admitted to a hospital in Abuja.
She developed symptoms on Wednesday 7 October, four days after arriving in the country, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).
Health authorities have begun contact-tracing to prevent further spread, with 44 close contacts of the woman identified.
Nigeria, the first West African state to report a case linked to the current Ebola crisis in East Africa, successfully stopped a previous outbreak in 2014.
Uganda's Ministry of Health has stressed there are currently no confirmed active Ebola cases in the country.
"We urge the public to remain calm, vigilant and to practice regular handwashing and sanitising," it said.
Is Ebola under control in Kenya after nine cases confirmed?
What is Ebola and why is stopping the latest outbreak so difficult?

Ebola is a rare but deadly disease, external caused by a virus. As the disease progresses, vomiting and diarrhoea develop and it can lead to organ failure. Some, but not all, patients develop internal and external bleeding.
The disease spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit.

The outbreak in Democratic Republic of Congo, which began in May, has claimed at least 4,600 lives, with more than 9,500 cases recorded, the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control reports, external.
It was caused by the Bundibugyo species of Ebola, which is relatively rare, with no approved vaccine or treatment - though trials are under way.
Shortly after the outbreak was announced, it was also reported in Uganda, where at least two people died. Uganda declared itself free of the disease in August after its last patient was discharged.
Following the latest case in Nigeria, Uganda's health ministry said preliminary information indicated that the patient had transited through Uganda without symptoms.

In a statement on X, Uganda's Director General of Health Services Charles Olaro said the woman had travelled to eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo for business before passing through Uganda in early October.
He said her symptoms had only developed after arriving in Nigeria.
The incubation period for Ebola ranges from two to 21 days, meaning those exposed to the virus may not become ill for several weeks.
The woman's exact travel history - key to tracing contacts - appears to be unclear at the moment.

"The location of exposure remains under investigation. The government of Nigeria is yet to provide detailed information on her travel itinerary and clinical history which will guide further investigations and any necessary contact tracing," Olaro said.
Nigeria's health minister confirmed the woman had had no symptoms when she arrived in Nigeria, but he said the patient had not confirmed travel to DR Congo.
"We presume that it was likely picked in Uganda," Pate told the national broadcaster Nigerian Television Authority (NTA) on Tuesday evening.
Her travel documents will be used to trace contacts and the authorities have urged the public to co-operate with health officials carrying out contact tracing.
The disease has also recently spread to Kenya, which has reported at least nine infections.
On Monday, the US advised its citizens to reconsider travel to Kenya because of health risks and raised its travel advisory level for the country.
Since the outbreak, Nigeria has stepped up disease surveillance, with the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control issuing public health advice to travellers.
The agency says travellers from countries with active or relevant Ebola transmission may be required to complete a health declaration form. Those arriving from other countries are currently exempt.
It has also urged travellers to remain vigilant and seek medical attention promptly if they develop symptoms of Ebola.
In 2014, Nigeria managed to beat an outbreak of Ebola which caused at least eight deaths.

articles.title: Sudan army drones hit mourners and fuel market killing more than 300 people, sources say
articles.summary: A truck carrying people to a funeral and a market alleged to be supplying fuel to the RSF were targeted.
body: Ameth Bek Hospital in Abyei town has been treating people wounded in Monday's attack on the market
Sudan's army has been accused of launching several drone strikes that have reportedly killed more than 300 people, including dozens travelling to a funeral.

The death toll from strikes in two areas of West Kordofan state on Sunday evening was 150, sources told the Sudan War Observatory, which tracks the conflict that erupted in 2023 between the army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF).
In Abyei, a disputed border area between Sudan and South Sudan, 153 people were killed when drones hit a market on Monday, the region's information minister said.
A military source told the BBC the army had carried out the Abyei attack, saying the market was a fuel supply site for the RSF.

The attack has raised tensions between South Sudan and Sudan, which jointly administer Abyei, as they both claim ownership to the oil-rich region in a dispute that has remained unresolved since South Sudan ceded in 2011.
South Sudan has summoned Sudan's ambassador to lodge a formal protest. There are fears the conflict could spill across the border.
A simple guide to what is happening in Sudan
Drones hammer Sudan's gold and oil zone - the pivotal new front line
Despite a partial arms embargo on Sudan, foreign countries have been supplying both the army and the RSF with drones and they are increasingly becoming the weapon of choice in the conflict.
The war has created one of the worst humanitarian crises in the world, killed hundreds of thousands of people and forced more than 14 million from their homes.

"We are alarmed by the continued deadly drone strikes across the country that are killing civilians, including children, and that are disrupting essential services," UN spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric said on Monday, external.
The rising use of armed drones came as 20 million people faced acute hunger, with a rising risk of famine in parts of the western region of Darfur and Greater Kordofan, he said.
Greater Kordofan comprises three states and is a vital axis linking Darfur, controlled by the RSF, to the capital, Khartoum, now in army hands.
The wave of drone attacks started on Sunday evening and, according to the Sudan War Observatory, it is likely they were launched from the army-held city of Kadugli in South Kordofan state.
A truck carrying around 200 mourners which had travelled from an area north of Abyei was hit as it arrived in the town of Al-Dabab in West Kordofan, the monitoring group said.
Sources told the group that 145 people were killed and a tent where mourners at the funeral had gathered was also hit, killing five others. A further 150 people were injured in the attacks, it said.

Army drones also bombed a market in the town of Al-Mujlad in West Kordofan on the same evening, according to the Sudan War Observatory, which said the exact number of deaths and injuries were not yet known.
Sudan's army has not responded to the allegation it carried out these strikes, but said it did not attack civilians even if they believed there were RSF fighters amongst them.

The attack in Abyei, which borders West Kordofan, took place on Monday around 11:30 local time (09:30 GMT) targeting Amiet Market around 10km (six miles) from Abyei town, the region's Information Minister Yohana Akol Ngor told Radio Tamazuj, which broadcasts from the Netherlands to audiences on the Sudan-South Sudan border.
On Tuesday, the minister confirmed to the Associated Press and Reuters that the death toll had risen from 73 to 153 people.
"It is a horrible and shocking situation," AP quotes him as saying.

BBC Verify has studied satellite images that show extensive burnt buildings in the north-east corner of Amiet Market, which is also known in Arabic as Al-Na'am Market. Older images from the area show it is usually full of trucks.

It has also verified footage filmed near the market that shows a large plume of smoke, at least one petrol tanker and someone talking about five missiles being fired. Another verified video shows two massive, separate fires coming from buildings near that section of the market.
This screengrab is from a video taken 600m from Amiet Market
Earlier, Ngor told Reuters that emergency workers had struggled to retrieve the bodies because of fires caused by the strikes.
On Monday, medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) said it had also received people wounded in the attack at Ameth Bek Hospital in Abyei town.

"So far we received over 20 patients, including several critical cases. Patients with burns were also admitted. We are providing surgical services and wound dressing, along with other emergency care," MSF's Christian Lindauer, the charity's manager at the hospital, said in a statement.
Meanwhile, a drone strike near the airport in Khartoum on Monday has killed four people, including three children, the AFP news agency reports, quoting a medical source.
It also cited a military source as saying air defences in the Sudanese capital had downed several other drones launched by the RSF towards the airport.
Fighting in Kordofan, a strategic area rich in gold and oil, has intensified over the last year after the army regained control of Khartoum from the RSF.
