“Burnham faces climate revolt after approval of North Sea gas drilling”, is the Guardian’s front page today.

The Telegraph has “Teachers face ban on Palestine badges”, Times leads with “Mahmood’s fight to save her migrant crackdown”. The FT runs “AI debt nerves trigger race for default insurance in case boom turns to bust”, the Mirror has “Tories’ cruel Covid car home ‘lie’”, and the i Paper says “Man City paid council £750,000 a year for stadium naming rights – that sold for £100m”.

On Prince Harry, the Sun splashes “I want to work it out … some people don’t”, the Mail writes “Oh, do put a sock in it Harry!”, and the Express has “Harry’s ‘some people don’t want it to work out’ dig”.
Helen Haines loses leg after being attacked with car

A man has been charged after the Australian MP Helen Haines was allegedly attacked with a car outside her electorate office in the state of Victoria. Haines, who is an independent MP, has lost one leg as a result of the incident and surgeons were fighting on Tuesday to save the other leg. Police say 43-year-old Brendan Nugent has been charged with dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury and causing harm to a commonwealth public official. Annie Kelly speaks to Guardian Australia political editor Tom McIlroy.
A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad

Ghent’s new €20m (£17m) design museum is a gleaming monument to recycling. Designed by London-based architects Carmody Groarke, it was built using everything from car windscreens, seaweed and old toilets to rubble dug straight from the building site.

Its bricks, many of which were pressed by the public during a two-day festival, are made of pulverised construction waste and hydrated lime. As well as saving two-thirds of the embodied carbon of a regular fired clay brick, they will continue to absorb CO2 from the atmosphere in the coming years, as the lime cures.

“We’re not claiming this is … a solution to the climate crisis,” says Sian Ricketts, Carmody Groarke’s sustainability lead. “But it is a sort of 82,000-brick proof of concept that you can do something different.”
Sign up here for a weekly roundup of The Upside, sent to you every Sunday
And finally, the Guardian’s puzzles are here to keep you entertained throughout the day. Until tomorrow.

articles.title: Battle over Meta’s alleged Bolsonaro bias intensifies days before Brazil presidential runoff
articles.summary: Lula’s supporters suspect tech firm meddling on behalf of US president Donald Trump, who has close ties to Bolsonaro family
body: Five days after his defeat in the first round of the Brazilian presidential election, leftwing president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva spent almost 24 hours unable to boost his Instagram posts, while his opponent, far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro, could.

Lula’s lawyers included the episode in a list of incidents that they submitted to the electoral court and international observers as “evidence” that Meta, Instagram’s owner, was actively trying to interfere in Brazil’s election in Bolsonaro’s favour.

Reports from Lula supporters saying their content had been removed or its reach restricted flooded social media in Brazil, while about a dozen watchdogs and research groups published reports describing what they called “indications” that Meta may have favoured the senator’s campaign.
Meta called Lula’s allegations “false and unfounded”, saying there had been “technical incidents” that affected campaigns from “different parts of the political spectrum”.

The controversy fuelled the electoral battle between Lula and Bolsonaro just days before next Sunday’s runoff and gained further traction after the electoral court ordered Meta not to give the candidates “unequal treatment”.
Related: Brazil cuts work week to 40 hours in win for Lula ahead of runoff

Late last week, justice Marco Aurélio Bellizze said he had found no evidence of deliberate action by the company, which would require further investigation, but he gave Meta 24 hours to prove that the problems affecting Lula had been fixed and would not happen again.

On Monday, after saying the company had failed to do so, Bellizze gave Meta a further 24 hours. The company responded on Tuesday, again denying any favouritism and saying it had introduced human review to prevent any automated restrictions.

Meta’s oversight board, a quasi-independent body whose decisions are binding, issued a statement saying it was “concerned by recurring enforcement failures in Meta’s election integrity efforts”, citing both Brazil’s election and the suspension of the anti-Trump No Kings movement’s account in the US for several hours last Saturday, during demonstrations aimed at encouraging early voting in the midterm elections.
The company said it suspended the No Kings account after its anti-fraud systems wrongly flagged what they believed was bot traffic, and apologised.

The board said it had seen the same pattern in Brazil, where there had been an “over-enforcement of Meta’s fraud policies against Brazil’s President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s ad accounts” on 23 September, when his campaign advertising account was disabled for more than an hour. Meta said this had happened “by mistake … and not for political reasons” after an anti-fraud review wrongly classified an ad as an attempt to impersonate a government social programme.

The board said: “From the removal of political activist accounts during protests in the US ahead of the midterm elections to technical restrictions that hit the accounts of a presidential candidate in Brazil leading to allegations of electoral interference, it’s clear that Meta must do more to ensure that its enforcement practices during elections are transparent and consistent, and that political speech is protected rather than stifled”.

João Victor Archegas, the coordinator at the thinktank Institute for Technology and Society, said it was “almost impossible” to prove any interference by Meta in Brazilian elections because only the company has access to its internal data, meaning there is no real external scrutiny, either from the electoral court or from the watchdogs producing reports on it.

“What we have so far is a collection of cases that perhaps one day we can piece together and reach some conclusion one way or the other. But today, because of the lack of information, unfortunately we cannot be certain,” he said.

Platforms such as Google and TikTok are not allowing political advertising in this election, leaving Meta’s services as the only large-scale channels for paid digital campaigning, which so far has earned the company £43m, 85% more than it made during the last presidential election.

A report by the watchdog CTRL+Z, founded by a former executive at Meta’s WhatsApp, catalogued 1,121 reports of lost or suppressed reach, restrictions on reposting, and account bans and blocks affecting mostly leftwing profiles. Meta dismissed it as a catalogue of anecdotes and users’ perceptions.

Media outlets posted examples of an experiment in which WhatsApp’s AI assistant refused to generate artwork featuring “Lula” and his ballot number, but did so for “Flávio” – Brazilians widely refer to the senator by his first name, reserving the surname for his father, former president Jair Bolsonaro.
The company said this reflected “a specific gap in our safeguards, not political bias” and that AI artwork could be generated using Lula’s first name, Luiz, with his ballot number.

Many Lula supporters raised suspicions that Meta was allegedly acting on behalf of the US president, Donald Trump, who has close ties to the Bolsonaro family and whom Lula has accused of trying to interfere in Brazil’s election.
Related: Lula says Trump wants to ‘colonise’ and capture Brazil’s resources by meddling in election

Lula’s lawyers appeared to embrace that argument, describing Meta in their filing to the electoral court as a “foreign company aligned with the Trump administration” that was acting as a “vector of external pressure on the [Brazilian] electorate”, without, however, offering any evidence of possible US involvement.

In the 9 October episode in which Lula’s campaign was temporarily unable to boost posts on Instagram, which 70% of Brazilian adults say they use as their primary source of information, his lawyers said that “silencing” the incumbent’s social media while his opponent’s continued operating normally created an unfair advantage for Bolsonaro.

The company said the problem affected only new posts, while older ones could still be promoted, and that it had been a “global outage” affecting “thousands of advertisers in different countries”, though Bolsonaro’s campaign was not among them.

Meta added: “We apply the same rules to all candidates, parties and political viewpoints in Brazil, just as we do in elections around the world. We do not suppress content to harm one side or give preferential treatment to any side.”

NetLab, a research laboratory on the internet and social media at the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro, produced a report showing that Meta allowed at least 1,600 election ads to be boosted from outside Brazil, something prohibited under Brazilian law.

Débora Salles, NetLab’s general coordinator, said they had not identified political bias towards either side, but that the failure “shows how the company repeatedly fails to ensure safety and compliance with electoral law”.

On the eve of the vote, NetLab identified paid ads that posed as official posts from the electoral court and contained false information that encouraged abstention, claiming that if it was raining, voters could cast their ballots online, which is not possible in Brazil.

“Regardless of whether a candidacy is being helped or harmed, what we see is that the company has difficulty complying with Brazilian electoral law and ends up undermining the integrity of the electoral process,” said Salles.

articles.title: Residents of ‘1066 Country’ lose battle for Bayeux tapestry tickets
articles.summary: Exclusive: East Sussex MP Helena Dollimore says ‘shambolic’ museum phone line has made her constituents lose out to ‘queue jumpers’
body: Hastings residents have missed out on tickets for the Bayeux tapestry after being put on hold for hours by a “glitchy and shambolic” phone system, their MP has said.

People from “1066 Country” were promised a chance to buy before a sales line opened to the public on Wednesday. But Helena Dollimore, the MP for Hastings and Rye, said it has been almost impossible for her constituents to get through to the British Museum.

VIP guests including Maya Jama, Mick Jagger and senior staff at Samsung and Bloomberg have had no such issues gaining access to Bayeux viewings, having attended star-studded events held in the tapestry room since September.

Hastings residents were told they could get early access to book the latest release of tickets from Monday this week by calling the British Museum box office and providing proof of their address. But Dollimore said her constituents were left on hold for hours.
“Why do my constituents have to work on a glitchy phone line when online booking is clearly possible for others?” she asked.
“One person booked after two hours and 38 minutes in the queue, another said he was on hold for two and a half hours.
“If you can’t get access right for the people in the place this tapestry tells the story of, you need to sort that out before you start letting people jump the queue.”

Celebrities, businesspeople and politicians flocked to the museum on Saturday for a ball. The guest of honour, tech billionaire Igor Tulchinsky, posed next to Rosanna Konarzewski, a communications executive who was wearing a sweeping ballgown made of a replica Bayeux tapestry. Sources in attendance said that while the general public have been banned from taking pictures of the embroidery, some ball guests managed to photograph it.

The Guardian revealed that another tech billionaire, Peter Thiel, was given a VIP tour of the embroidery before it opened to the public. Guests of the One Aldwych hotel are also allowed to view the tapestry if they book a £1,000-a-night room.

Dollimore said: “I had a constituent who waited for hours with her elderly parent who was in her 80s, and they were sent away because of a corporate event. They promised the people of 1066 Country would be able to get access to the tapestry, but seem to be prioritising these corporates.”
The MP has unsuccessfully tried to get tickets for herself and her family. “I have been trying since 10am to get through, and even I can’t,” she said.
The MP managed to secure access to the tapestry for schoolchildren across Hastings after lobbying the museum. “To be fair to the museum, that has been a success,” she said.

Members of the public faced online queues of up to nine hours when tickets went on sale for the first time this summer. There were reports of 40,000 people queueing by mid-morning, with that figure ballooning to almost 80,000 by mid-afternoon.
The 70-metre (229ft) tapestry, which is made of linen with embroidered images of events surrounding the Battle of Hastings in 1066, arrived in the UK in July for the first time in nearly 1,000 years.
Adult tickets cost £33 in peak hours and £27 at other times, compared with the €12 (£10) fee at the artwork’s home in Bayeux, Normandy.

A British Museum spokesperson said: “Demand for the Bayeux tapestry exhibition has been exceptionally high. In recognition of the area’s historic connection to the Battle of Hastings we agreed to offer residents the chance to secure tickets before their wider release.
“This offer is not guaranteed access – it is on a first-come, first-served basis in the same way tickets for the exhibition are on sale to our members and the public.
“All residents are still able to book tickets as part of the general sale on 21 October and will have further opportunities in the new year when the third tranche of tickets are released.”
• This article was amended on 21 October 2026. An earlier version incorrectly described Rosanna Konarzewski as the “host” of a Bayeux tapestry ball held at the British Museum.

articles.title: Fifth foreign firm pulls out of controversial Israeli cable car project to East Jerusalem
articles.summary: Rights groups say the planned 1.4km route, which ends at compound run by far-right settler group Elad, will displace Palestinians and reshape the cultural landscape
body: A fifth foreign company has pulled out of a plan to build a cable car from West to East Jerusalem that threatens to involve the seizure of land and property rights from dozens of Palestinian families along its route, but local authorities insist the scheme is proceeding as planned.

The project appeared to have stalled for four years until late September, just weeks before Israel’s 27 October elections, when the Jerusalem Development Authority (JDA) issued a notice of intent to award a contract without a public tender to ROPES, a cable car engineering consultancy based in South Tyrol, Italy.
However, Stephan Obexer, chief executive of ROPES told the Guardian his company had declined the consultancy work because of another commitment in India.

The 1.4km cable car route, approved by the Israeli government in 2019 and upheld by the high court in 2022, would connect West Jerusalem to a planned 16,000 sq metres tourist complex promoted by Elad, a settler organisation seeking to consolidate Israeli control over Palestinian areas of occupied East Jerusalem.

The Israeli occupation of the Palestinian territories began in 1967 and the Old City and the rest of the eastern half of Jerusalem were fully annexed in 1980, although they are still considered occupied under international law.
Related: Israel accused of trying to ‘eliminate’ living conditions for Palestinians in West Bank

According to Emek Shaveh, an Israeli NGO, the JDA had recently accelerated plans for a long-delayed cable car through occupied East Jerusalem, where Israel’s continued presence has been ruled unlawful by the international court of justice, in a project once described by former Jerusalem mayor Nir Barkat as a way for visitors to “understand who is truly the landlord of the city”.

‘‘This project threatens the Palestinian communities and the timeless landscape of Jerusalem’s historic core,’’ said Emek Shaveh in a recent statement. ‘‘It is clear that the project’s central motivation is to consolidate the settlers’ hold in those areas as part of an effort to displace Palestinians from the Historic Basin and reshape Jerusalem’s cultural landscape.’’
The plan comes amid escalating settler violence and efforts to seize Palestinian land across the occupied territories.

At least four foreign companies – three French and one Swiss – have expressed interest in the project, but several have withdrawn over its political sensitivity, according to Haaretz, an Israeli newspaper. In 2015, the French government urged one company not to participate. Another French company, CNA, pulled out less than a year ago, followed more recently by Switzerland’s Histec Engineering.
ROPES did not respond to a request for a written statement or questions about whether legal concerns over the project’s location in occupied East Jerusalem had influenced its decision.
The JDA did not respond to the Guardian’s request for comment.

But a spokesperson for the JDA told Haaretz: “Following the high court of justice’s dismissal of petitions against the project about a year and a half ago, the cable car continues to proceed according to plan and in accordance with the timetables set. Steps to promote the project are subject to the mandatory tenders law, and the tender is expected to be ready for publication in the coming months once its formulation is completed.”
Related: Israeli settlers attack European diplomats in West Bank

The move has sparked protests from Israeli heritage and environmental groups and Palestinians in Silwan, an East Jerusalem neighbourhood at the foot of the Old City, who warn that the project threatens Palestinian heritage in territory they seek for a future state and would see cable cars passing just metres above their homes.

“The cable car stands in complete contradiction to the historic principle that no large buildings or infrastructure should be built around the Old City,’’ says Alon Arad, an archaeologist and the executive director of Emek Shaveh. ‘‘It is particularly troubling that the Israel Nature and Parks Authority, the body responsible for upholding this principle, is cooperating with the project.

“To understand the political context, one must look at the route: it begins in West Jerusalem and ends at a compound run by the far-right settler organisation Elad Foundation, which stands to benefit from a project costing the state around half a billion shekels. Elad is notorious for using state resources to advance its political agenda in East Jerusalem, taking over Palestinian properties, evicting families and settling Jewish residents in their place.”
The Elad Foundation, which does not appear to be formally involved in the project, did not respond to the Guardian’s request for comment.

According to rights groups, the cable car project directly threatens about 54 Palestinian homes along its route in the Wadi Hilweh neighbourhood in Silwan, with the expropriation of either land or air rights, and indirectly threatens many others in the vicinity. Israeli authorities have issued 17 expropriation notices covering about 8.7 dunams (2.15 acres) of land along the proposed route, where pylons supporting the cable car would be erected.

“These buildings, home to roughly 450 residents, lie directly beneath the proposed route,” said Sari Kronish, an architect and director of the East Jerusalem department at Bimkom, an Israeli planning rights organisation. “Cable cars would pass as close as four metres above rooftops and near residential windows, violating residents’ privacy and restricting future development. Expropriations of land and homes for support pillars have already been set in motion, leaving residents in a constant state of uncertainty.”
Reached by the Guardian, the Israel Nature and Parks Authority said: “Our involvement was limited to providing feedback on the proposed alternatives.”

Across occupied East Jerusalem, Israeli settlers are increasingly taking over Palestinian properties, while authorities have stepped up demolitions of homes lacking building permits, displacing families. The Mount of Olives, home to some of Christianity’s holiest sites, has also become a target of settler expansion, raising concerns among churches that own land there.

The campaign has intensified since the war in Gaza started in October 2023 amid accelerating land seizures and settlement expansion across the occupied West Bank, where more than 1,100 Palestinians have been killed by Israeli forces or settlers.

Settler violence has surged during the annual olive harvest. On 16 October, settlers attacked Palestinian villages, burning cars and trees and injuring a Washington Post photographer. The following day, settlers attacked European diplomats, a French mayor and Palestinian olive pickers, injuring three people and damaging a diplomatic vehicle.

articles.title: Drone strike kills more than 150 at market in Sudanese war
articles.summary: The strike pushed the toll from attacks in recent days to more than 250, underscoring the lethality of Sudan’s war that ⁠erupted in April 2023
body: A drone strike on a market in a border region disputed by Sudan and South Sudan killed at least 153 people on Monday, according to a local official, the latest in a wave of deadly attacks.

The strike pushed the toll from attacks in recent days to more than 250, underscoring the lethality of airstrikes in Sudan’s war, which ⁠erupted in April 2023 between the Sudanese Armed Forces ⁠and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF).
Yohanna Akol Ngor, the Abyei administration’s caretaker information minister, blamed Sudan’s military, without providing evidence, for Monday’s attack on Amiet market, north of Abyei town.
Related: Deaths, disappearances and forced recruitment: refugees recount horrors of relentless war in Sudan
“We have recorded 153 deaths,” Akol said.
Sudan’s military did not respond to a request for comment.
A witness said he heard five large explosions that led to a fuel depot nearby catching fire.

“People started evacuating the casualties. They ​had injuries from shrapnel on their stomach and legs … In one site, I saw 28 bodies that were burnt,” the witness said, asking not to be named for safety reasons.

Doctors Without Borders, known by its French acronym MSF, said more than 20 wounded people were brought to Ameth Bek hospital, where MSF teams were working alongside staff from South Sudan’s health ministry.
“So far we received over 20 patients, including several critical cases. Patients with burns were also admitted,” said Dr Christian Lindauer, MSF’s medical activities manager at the hospital.

South Sudan’s foreign ministry also blamed Sudan’s military, saying it had summoned Sudan’s ambassador to protest and urged Sudan to “refrain from any actions that endanger civilian lives and property”.

South Sudan declared independence from Sudan in 2011. Since then, both countries have staked a claim to oil-rich Abyei, which is jointly administered. It borders Sudan’s Kordofan region, which has become a major centre of fighting in the war.
On Sunday, a drone strike killed 80 people, mostly commuters catching rides home, when it hit near a market in West Kordofan state.
Another attack ⁠on a market in RSF stronghold Nyala killed 23 people and injured 44 on Friday, according to volunteers there.
MSF called on all parties to stop attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure, expressing concern about people’s ability to safely reach healthcare and other essential services.
Amiet market is a trading hub serving the Ngok Dinka and Misseriya communities.

The region’s majority Ngok Dinka population favours joining South Sudan, while Misseriya nomads who use its pastures favour Sudan. Abyei has also experienced deadly communal violence, including fighting over land between Ngok Dinka and neighbouring Twic Dinka communities.

articles.title: Sanae Takaichi took on Japan’s male-dominated politics and won – can she survive a second year in power?
articles.summary: The straight-talking PM’s ability to manage Trump and stand up to China have endeared her to the public, but she may need friends closer to home to survive
body: Visitors squeeze into the kiosk near Japan’s national diet building to snap up souvenirs bearing the face of Sanae-chan, the affectionate nickname for the country’s leader: chocolate biscuits, dango sweets, stickers and document files proclaiming that “Japan is back”.
“The Takaichi range is incredibly popular,” says a member of staff.
As Sanae Takaichi marks a year since she upended Japan’s male-dominated politics, the country’s first female prime minister has defied predictions that her time in office would be short-lived.

Instead, the straight-talking conservative has rewritten the rulebook on Japanese leadership, led her troubled Liberal Democratic party (LDP) to a resounding election victory, and won support among voters for refusing to back down during a prolonged row with China over Taiwan.
“Takaichi’s direct style has been an asset … particularly in her diplomatic strategy,” says Sheila A Smith, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations in New York.

Recent opinion polls put Takaichi’s approval rating at around 50% – the lowest ⁠level since she ⁠took ​office, but still a robust number for a Japanese leader 12 months into their term, and comfortably clear of the 30% “danger zone” that has signalled the end of previous administrations.

She has won plaudits for her refusal to back down in a diplomatic row with China, while her strong social media presence has helped her connect with younger voters disillusioned with the more analogue political style of her predecessors.

But the 65-year-old protege of the assassinated former prime minister Shinzo Abe marks her anniversary in October at the most precarious point of her premiership. Takaichi is battling the fallout from her first major cabinet scandal, mounting economic pressures and doubts about how she will fund a proposed cut in the consumption tax. She also faces persistent questioning about her work style, including her relationship with party colleagues and the media, and claims that she gets by on minimal sleep.

As the leader of a country with a long security relationship with the US, Takaichi has gone out of her way to endear herself to Donald Trump during their four meetings since she became prime minister. She chose not to respond to his quip about Pearl Harbor when they met in the Oval Office in March, although her body language suggested she was far from impressed.

Awkward moments notwithstanding, she has managed to keep Japan’s relationship with its most important ally on an even keel – even declaring the dawn of a “golden age” between Tokyo and Washington soon after she became prime minister.
At home, however, she faces the strongest political headwinds of her premiership to date.

This month, she initially defended her agricultural minister, Kazuo Yana, who provoked anger for remarks about cutting road funding in municipalities that didn’t support him. Takaichi’s response to pressure for his removal was typically idiosyncratic, describing Yana’s reported comments as “quite honestly, lame,” if true. Pressure built, and on 14 October Yana became the first cabinet minister in her government to resign.

“Takaichi may pay some price for the scandal in forthcoming opinion polls,” says Tobias Harris, founder of the political risk advisory firm Japan Foresight, adding that she had stood by him for almost two weeks while the scandal brewed.

Her current troubles don’t end with Yana. She has been accused of pushing through revisions that practically rule out a change in Japan’s male-only succession law, despite the public’s enthusiasm for a reigning empress, and offered muted backing for Tomoko Akane, the Japanese head of the international criminal court, which has been targeted with sanctions by Trump. She also faces mounting anger in Okinawa following the arrest this month of a US marine suspected of murdering and robbing a local woman.
I expect her successors will need to adapt and follow her lead

“She will need to handle slip-ups by cabinet members, hurdles in keeping her coalition partner satisfied and, most importantly, continuing consumer concerns about cost-of-living pressures,” says Smith.

Doubts persist over Takaichi’s plans to ease financial pressures across Japan – a two-year reduction in the consumption tax on food and drink from 8% to 1%, and cash payments to struggling households.
Takaichi insists the measure won’t require more borrowing, but has failed to explain how they will be funded, adding to concerns about Japan’s public debt, already the highest among G7 economies.
Supporters revel in her direct style of communicating, but it has triggered accusations that she is avoiding media scrutiny.

Takaichi rarely grants individual interviews, preferring to explain policies, often in great detail, in posts on X. In her first five months in office, she gave 34 press briefings, fewer than her immediate predecessors Shigeru Ishiba, with 57, and Fumio Kishida, with 90, held over a comparable period. In that time she wrote 370 posts on X, according to the Kyodo news agency.

The tradition of holding background briefings with newspaper and TV executives has fallen by the wayside, says a senior editor at a Japanese weekly magazine who asked not to be named. “She has been aggressive towards the legacy media since day one, something I think she learned from Donald Trump.”

Takaichi’s gamble on the consumption tax, and her belated condemnation of Yana’s alleged comments, point to possible turbulence ahead, according to some observers, leaving her vulnerable to plotting by the same party colleagues who helped put her in the prime minister’s office.
Related: Japan sees largest protest in support of pacifist constitution as PM Takaichi pushes revisions

While her predecessors built alliances over dinner at exclusive ryotei restaurants, Takaichi prefers to spend her evenings at home with her husband, Taku Yamamoto, a former lower house lawmaker who suffered a stroke last year. However, she does enjoy a cigarette, perhaps accompanied by a blast of Smoke On the Water by one of her favourite bands, Deep Purple.

She met colleagues over meals only five times in her first six months in office, according to the Mainichi Shimbun newspaper, significantly fewer than her predecessors. Abe, by contrast, hosted 50 gatherings over a similar period, and Fumio Kishida 35, including several during the Covid-19 pandemic. “It’s usual for Japanese prime ministers to hang out with other politicians in the evening and decide on policy,” says the magazine editor.

Takaichi, who vowed to “work, work, work” on behalf of voters, claims she gets only two to four hours of sleep a night, and sometimes summons aides in the early hours of the morning. Security protocols reportedly mean she is forbidden from going shopping, although her husband told a Japanese monthly magazine that he is occasionally permitted to order a pizza, adding that the couple stockpile microwaved ready meals and instant noodles. “In the morning, I have a bath, make breakfast and then wash the dishes, not to mention putting on my makeup,” she told MPs this week. “I feel like I’m spending three or four more hours than male prime ministers doing these things.”
Harris, Abe’s English-language biographer, says there were “notable differences” in style between Japan’s longest-serving prime minister and his protege.

“Takaichi is clearly more isolated, refusing in-person briefings from bureaucrats, having fewer meals with political allies and business representatives, and generally relying on her own judgment and perhaps not hearing as wide a range of views as her predecessors,” he says.
Testy relations with the media will not cause her to lose sleep as long as her message resonates with voters.

Smith says Takaichi’s “willingness to provide clear, no-nonsense responses to difficult policy challenges”, including the need for Japan to raise defence spending and improve its ability to respond to threats from China and North Korea, is likely to keep many voters on side: “I expect her successors will need to adapt and follow her lead,” she adds.

As long as that approach continues to work, even sceptical members of the LDP hierarchy who may wince at her personal style – sharing a laugh with Donald Trump at Joe Biden’s expense or serenading Italian prime minister Giorgia Meloni – will continue to back her. What that means for her political longevity is less clear.

“She has a reputation for trusting her own advice and not building up a strong cadre of loyalists … and not playing the LDP’s social game,” says Harris. “That may endear her to voters, but it risks leaving her with few friends if her circumstances take a negative turn.”

articles.title: Ukraine war briefing: US envoy Witkoff to meet Putin after ‘constructive’ talks with Zelenskyy in Norway
articles.summary: Talks in Oslo made ‘meaningful progress’ toward engaging Russia, a US official said. What we know on day 1,701
body: US envoy Steve Witkoff will meet Russian president Vladimir Putin on Wednesday after what a US official called “constructive” talks with Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Norway. The US official said Ukraine brought forward new ideas and proposals to the Oslo talks, which also involved the leaders of Norway and Finland ⁠and European and Nato representatives, and that participants made “meaningful ⁠progress” toward a coordinated approach to engaging Russia.

The official, who ​spoke to Reuters on the condition of anonymity, said the talks covered “key elements of a comprehensive peace framework”, including security guarantees for Ukraine, a postwar economic plan and a broader European security architecture. Witkoff would aim to “create a pathway toward direct trilateral and broader multilateral negotiations”, the official said. US president Donald ⁠Trump on Tuesday ⁠called ​on Ukraine to make a deal ⁠to settle the war with Russia. “Ukraine has to ⁠want to settle this ​war,” Trump ‌told reporters.

Zelenskyy travelled to Oslo seeking to repair relations with Washington, which have sunk to new lows. Trump’s recent gestures toward Moscow, including a deal to buy Russian diesel and a waiver of new sanctions, have sparked bipartisan pushback in the US Congress and worry in European capitals. Zelenskyy said he had ​discussed “Article 5-like” security guarantees, referring to the Nato stipulation that an attack on one ally is an attack on all. “I am ‌thankful to the American side that they underlined again that it will ‌be strong,” he said.

Elon Musk last week ordered the slowdown of a military-grade ⁠version of SpaceX’s Starlink satellite service that Ukraine relies on, the Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday, citing US ⁠officials and people familiar ⁠with the ​matter. Musk, SpaceX and the White House did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment. Ukraine uses the service – known as Starshield – for battlefield communications and drone operations. Restricting the satellite service hampered the country’s attack and air ⁠defence drone missions against Russia.

US defence secretary Pete Hegseth meanwhile insisted Tuesday that the Pentagon had not directed any changes to Starshield, saying: “We haven’t pulled anything back.” “Nothing’s changed from our view. We haven’t made any directives or anything like that,” he said. On Friday, Trump said he did not request any curbs to Starshield. “It wasn’t me. And I don’t think it was Elon,” Trump said. Musk previously said that “any limits on speed or usage” of Starshield systems were “decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS.”

Nato said Tuesday it was deploying additional planes, drones and radar systems to the Black Sea after a string of attacks on ships near Romania and Bulgaria in the latest spillover from Russia’s war on Ukraine. “Allies have or will send additional maritime patrol aircraft, radar systems, explosive exploitation teams, intelligence personnel, drones, and more to the Black Sea,” said Col Martin O’Donnell, a Nato spokesperson. “The most important thing we can do, however, is to increase our situational awareness in the region through increased sensors and data sharing,” he added.

The ⁠Russian military ⁠struck ​three cargo vessels in Ukraine’s ⁠port of Reni and two ⁠other cargo vessels en ​route ‌to ‌Odesa, Russia’s defence ‌ministry said on Tuesday. Russian forces also hit two logistics hubs in ‌the Volyn region and in the ​city of Khmelnitskiy, it said, adding that ⁠the vessels and hubs ​were ​all being ​used for ​military ‌purposes. Russia also unleashed another missile and drone blitz of civilian areas in Ukraine on Tuesday, killing at least nine people, officials said.

The Kremlin said Tuesday that work was under way to ease ⁠the humanitarian ⁠situation ​in the Russian-controlled town of Oleshky in southern ⁠where residents have reported a worsening food crisis. Kremlin spokesperson ⁠Dmitry Peskov said ‌Putin had ‌discussed the situation in Oleshky with Trump and told him that Russia’s human rights commissioner was engaged on the issue.

articles.title: Italy to deploy 500 troops to Milan after days of protests and looting
articles.summary: Government planning tougher security measures as France also says military forces will be deployed
body: Italy’s government is sending 500 soldiers to Milan and vowed a “firm response from the state” after protests against the cost of living descended into clashes with police, vandalism and looting. Further demonstrations are planned on Saturday.

The government of the far-right prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, also announced new security measures, including an offence of violent participation in ⁠a demonstration, tougher penalties for ⁠rioters, and financial liability for ​parents whose children take part in vandalism and looting.

In France, the interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, said on Tuesday some military forces would be deployed during ⁠protests ​planned for this Saturday, “mostly to free police and gendarmes in their mission to maintain order”.

The French prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, told parliament that the police presence during Saturday’s demonstrations ⁠would be “massive” and that ​his ​goal was ​for an “immediate return ​to order” ‌after last weekend’s violent riots.

Lecornu will meet with representatives from five unions on Wednesday morning to discuss security, according to a letter sent to the organisations and reviewed by AFP, which noted some were attempting to subvert the protests with “unacceptable acts”. School students have not been invited to the meeting.

Police in Milan, in northern Italy, detained 271 young people after hooded youths set bins ablaze, ransacked shops and smashed windows, including in the area surrounding the city’s cathedral, during the unrest on Saturday and Sunday.

Police used teargas and water cannon to disperse the violent groups, who were on the fringes of an initially peaceful protest. Of those detained, 32 have been arrested, including 23 minors and 13 foreign nationals, police said on Monday. A further 28 people were reported to judicial authorities.

Images of Saturday’s clashes in France, including mobs looting shops and public buildings set on fire, prompted several countries including the US, China and Germany to issue travel advice for their citizens. Nearly 2,400 people were arrested in one of France’s most violent recent bouts of unrest.

French authorities on Monday announced partial curfews in several cities, including Paris, Bordeaux, Lille and Nice, and after a night of relative calm, Lecornu said on Tuesday that new curfews would be imposed where they were needed.

Authorities in Paris renewed Monday night’s curfew, which would apply from 11pm on Tuesday until 6am on Wednesday to the Place de la République, where many of the weekend clashes took place, and in the central Les Halles shopping district.

Paris police ordered a temporary ban on people carrying cans or bottles of petrol or gas, and banned masks and helmets in some areas. A man was also arrested in connection with the burning down of the historic town hall in Limoges.

The Italian press agency Ansa reported that one of the security measures being considered in the country was aimed at second-generation immigrant youths, known as maranza – a slang term used to describe gangs of young people, usually from marginalised areas.
Many luxury stores in Milan’s fashion district have stayed closed amid fears of further unrest. Brands including Chanel, Tiffany ‌and Dior removed merchandise from ‌their windows as a precaution.
Other stores ransacked included the sports retailers Decathlon and Arc’teryx and the mobile phone operator Vodafone, footage showed.

“The government will respond firmly to these attacks on the state, ​including through measures aimed at curbing violence by minors,” the foreign minister, Antonio Tajani, who also serves as deputy prime minister, said after Meloni chaired a meeting with top security officials on Monday.

Meloni’s coalition, which is facing a general election next year, is reportedly planning tougher penalties for road blockades after days of protests in southern Italy by lorry drivers over fuel prices.
Related: Why are people protesting across Europe?

Meanwhile, Milan is bracing for further protests on Saturday after a new movement, called 17 October, emerged on social media. It said it would organise demonstrations there and in other Italian cities each Saturday afternoon “until this government of thieves collapses”.
“You are the violent ones,” the group said. “You, who denied us a future. Now, we are claiming that future ourselves.”

Opposition politicians often accuse the government of using security as a propaganda tool, arguing that Italy’s leaders do little to address core issues such as education, housing and living conditions in marginalised areas.

There were also tensions during protests at the weekend over the high cost of living in other northern Italian cities, ​including Bologna, Brescia, Bergamo ​and Turin, where 28 protesters were arrested, police said.
The protests in Italy and France have been mirrored by demonstrations in other parts of Europe.
Thousands rallied in Lisbon and other Portuguese cities on Tuesday evening, hours after police dismantled housing protest camps at dawn and arrested 55 people.
Demonstrators in Portugal are protesting soaring housing costs, seeking to align themselves with similar actions in neighbouring Spain, where tents have been set up in central Madrid for weeks.
In Lisbon, thousands of people gathered in the central Rossio square, where protesters voted by a show of hands to re-establish their tent camp from Wednesday.
“They forced me on to the streets to shout”, read one placard. Another declared: “Lisbon is not for sale”.

Anti-government demonstrations have also rocked the Albanian capital Tirana over the past week, driven by fresh demands for better university conditions, anger over corruption and a controversial resort development linked to Donald Trump’s family.

Clashes between the protesters and police escalated again on Tuesday amid renewed calls for prime minister Edi Rama’s resignation. Riot police used teargas and water cannon to disperse protesters who fired fireworks and hurled molotov cocktails and stones at officers.
Earlier on Tuesday, Rama repeated earlier accusations that “foreign actors” were to blame for the violence, having previously accused both Russia and Iran of driving online misinformation.

“It is a hybrid war that gains traction precisely because it is rooted in genuine grievances, not mere fantasy,” the prime minister said, citing the rising cost of living, housing affordability and concerns for the future.

articles.title: US has resumed sharing intelligence with Ukraine about Russian strikes, says Zelenskyy
articles.summary: Advance warnings of missile attacks were seemingly suspended last week by the White House, but Ukraine’s president says: ‘Now it works’
body: The US has resumed sharing intelligence with Kyiv about Russian missile strikes, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Tuesday after a meeting with the US envoy Steve Witkoff in Norway.

He said Ukraine was again receiving advance warnings of ballistic missile attacks, which were seemingly suspended last week by the White House. “Now it works. It’s great,” he said, adding that the US move would save lives.
The Ukrainian president said: “It’s very important for our people, for children, adults, civilians, because we can hear when ballistic [missiles] is coming. So we are thankful to the American side.”

Witkoff will on Wednesday meet Russian president Vladimir Putin after what a US official called “constructive” talks with Zelenskyy in Norway. The US envoy would aim to “create a pathway toward direct trilateral and broader multilateral negotiations”, a US official told Reuters.

The talks in Oslo took place amid the worst crisis in US-Ukraine relations since Putin’s full-scale invasion nearly five years ago. Donald Trump has bitterly accused Zelenskyy of failing to end the war and has said Ukraine needs a new leader.

On Tuesday Trump again suggested Zelenskyy was the main obstacle to an agreement. “We want Zelensky to make a deal. He can make a deal. He could have made a deal two years ago when we had our little chat in the Oval Office,” he said.
Trump also said he had asked Putin to release Stephen Hubbard – an American taken prisoner by Russian forces in occupied Ukraine – in a further sign of his growing public alliance with Moscow.

The US president’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner, joined Witkoff and Zelenskyy by video for the talks. Norway’s prime minister, Jonas Gahr Støre, and the Finnish president, Alexander Stubb, also took part, alongside EU and British security officials.

Zelenskyy said he had held a “positive” phone call earlier with the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio. Asked if Ukraine was now losing the war, after recent hostile US actions, Zelenskyy replied: “Of course we are not losing. But we are losing people because of Russian attacks and time. It’s a pity.”

He said he had raised with Rubio restrictions imposed last week on Starshield, the military-grade version of Elon Musk’s satellite internet service. The slowdown has crippled Ukraine’s ability to launch mid-range drone strikes on Russian battlefield positions.

Zelenskyy said he had offered to stop Ukraine’s long-range attacks on Russian oil refineries – a key Trump demand – if the US provided Kyiv with Patriot missile interceptors. The Pentagon has blocked the delivery of Patriots to Kyiv paid for by other countries, leaving Kyiv more vulnerable than ever to air attacks.

Speaking on Tuesday, Zelenskyy also said he opposed a trilateral summit floated by Putin, which would see the Russian leader, Trump and China’s president, Xi Jinping, meet next month to strike a Ukraine deal. Zelenskyy would be shut out, the Wall Street Journal reported.
“There can be nothing about Ukraine without Ukraine,” Zelenskyy said in Oslo. He added: “If it’s about Ukraine and our future it can only be acceptable when we are at the table of negotiations.”

The Washington-Kyiv crisis began 10 days ago when Trump announced he was lifting US sanctions on Russian diesel, in an attempt to lower fuel prices ahead of the US midterm elections. He then announced an energy ceasefire, which Kyiv implemented for several days but Russia ignored.

Despite this, Trump has bitterly rounded on Zelenskyy. He has effectively positioned the US as Russia’s ally, favouring Moscow over Kyiv, to the dismay of America’s pro-Ukrainian European and British backers. The US’s peace proposals have largely echoed Russia’s maximalist demands.

The EU’s foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, on Tuesday questioned whether US negotiators had been honest brokers in the peace efforts. Witkoff has held numerous meetings with Putin in Moscow, while so far visiting Kyiv only once.

“Although American negotiators have been trying to push Ukraine into surrender for … one and a half years now,” Ukraine has not surrendered on Putin’s terms “because Europe has been supporting Ukraine”, Kallas said.
Tuesday’s talks came after Zelenskyy told a bipartisan group of US politicians that he believed “some political decision has been made to slow down … support for us”.
US officials have denied this but have failed to explain convincingly why satellite communication services were curtailed or intelligence sharing temporarily cut off.

Speaking to reporters in India, Rubio insisted nothing had changed. He said Patriot interceptors were in short supply and were needed in other parts of the world, as well as for the US’s own defence. “There has not been some deliberate political directive to go out and harm Ukraine,” he insisted.

At least nine people were killed in Ukraine on Tuesday. They included passengers who were travelling on the Kyiv to Odesa highway. A Russian drone struck two vehicles, killing three people and injuring four. One of the victims was the driver of a shuttle bus, which was on its way from the capital to a military cemetery.

articles.title: RFK Jr’s ‘deities of vaccine research’ raided by police in Guinea-Bissau
articles.summary: Police seize doses of hepatitis B vaccine from people at center of dispute over research on African newborns
body: Controversial vaccine researchers who have been praised by Robert F Kennedy Jr, the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) secretary, had their offices in Guinea-Bissau raided by judicial police, who seized doses of hepatitis B vaccines, officials said on Facebook.

The researchers have been at the heart of an ongoing dispute over research on African newborns, supported by $1.6m from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and matched by the Pershing Square Foundation and the Bluebell Foundation for a total of $3.2m.

The police search took place on Monday, involving “investigative procedures aimed at clarifying the circumstances related to the said batch of vaccines”, according to the social media post, which was translated from Portuguese. The announcement noted that seizing the immunizations did not point to “irregularities in the quality, safety, or effectiveness of the vaccines”.

The Bandim Health Project recently posted a letter of approval for the trial from Guinea-Bissau’s national ethics committee at the ministry of public health, dated 14 July and signed by the committee’s president, Mouhammed Djicó Ould Ahmed. A Danish research ethics committee, which had to change its rules to consider a clinical trial, also approved the study earlier this month.
Quinhin Nantote, the health minister of Guinea-Bissau’s transitional government, disputed reports that the trial would move forward.
“This is not even remotely true,” Nantote told the Guardian in Portuguese on Thursday.

The study was redesigned over the summer, but it would still deny hepatitis B vaccines to 7,000 newborns in the first six weeks of life, in a country where about one in five adults have the virus. Hepatitis B kills 15% to 25% of people with chronic infections, causing cancer and liver failure, and newborns are particularly vulnerable – but vaccination within 24 hours of birth is safe and highly effective at preventing illness.

Any study that would deny the vaccine to participants was “unethical and exposes newborns to serious and potentially irreversible harm”, said Tarik Jašarević, a spokesperson for the World Health Organization (WHO), calling hepatitis B vaccination at birth an “essential public health intervention”.

Through its country office in Guinea-Bissau, the WHO and its partners have been advising the ministry of health on the planned introduction of the hepatitis B vaccine and the potential impact of this study, Jašarević added.
The Bandim Health Project was founded by anthropologist Peter Aaby in 1978, and it is now co-led by his wife, Christine Stabell Benn, an epidemiologist.

Kennedy has repeatedly praised their work, calling them “the deities of vaccine research” at a recent anti-vaccine conference. He has several times referenced the results of a study they conducted on the diphtheria-tetanus-pertussis (DTP), which the same researchers later conducted again and found completely different results. Even so, Kennedy called Aaby a “very famous” researcher on Joe Rogan’s podcast in 2023 and cited his research when he halted US funding to Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance.

Stabell Benn was a member of the hepatitis B working group of the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP), helping present evidence to the US committee that voted to end the universal birth recommendation before such decisions on vaccines were stayed by a federal judge. Stabell Benn also hosted a podcast with Tracy Beth Høeg, a former top official with the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) who said she wanted to end “unnecessary” vaccines.
Aaby, Stabell Benn and Frederik Schaltz-Buchholzer, the lead researcher on the project, did not respond to the Guardian’s questions about the trial and the police search.

The Bandim organization is deeply enmeshed in Guinea-Bissau but has done little to improve the country’s health and research capacities in five decades of operation, according to a report from the non-profit Stand Up for Science (SUFS). The organization is now fundraising to help roll out the vaccines at birth to all newborns in the country.

“Our investigator encountered significant distrust of Bandim by the citizenry of Guinea-Bissau,” said Colette Delawalla, an American health researcher and founder of SUFS. “However, because of the lack of public health infrastructure, Bandim is often the only option in situations where people are desperate to access medical care of any kind.”

The police raid underlines the fact that Guinea-Bissau is a “fragile” nation that experienced a military coup less than a year ago, Delawalla said. The country lacks the stability needed for clinical trials, she added.

“Guinea-Bissau is in the difficult situation of trying to protect their youth, their future, from exploitation by two powerful western nations and they are using what leverage they have to do so,” Delawalla said.

articles.title: Nato increases Black Sea deployment amid escalating deadly Russian attacks
articles.summary: Mounting anxiety as Russia’s war on Ukraine reaches Nato’s borders with targeting of vessels transporting agricultural cargo
body: Nato is deploying additional military assets to the Black Sea amid the recent deadly escalation of Russian attacks on merchant shipping, as five more vessels were attacked on Tuesday.
Russia’s military said it ⁠struck ​three cargo vessels in Ukraine’s ⁠port of Reni and two ⁠other cargo vessels en ​route ‌to ‌Odesa.

Russia’s targeting of vessels taking grain and other agricultural cargoes from Ukraine’s ports – central to the country’s economy – have brought the conflict to Nato’s borders, with a new high-risk designation used by the London shipping insurance market now covering all of the Black Sea save for the territorial waters of Romania, Bulgaria and Turkey.

With a sharply rising death toll among civilian seafarers that has made Black Sea routes the world’s most dangerous, Nato announced the ⁠defensive military alliance would add more surveillance assets in the region.

Nato’s spokesperson, Allison Hart, said: “Today, Nato ‌ambassadors met in ‌the North Atlantic Council to discuss security in the Black Sea. Nato has already ​strengthened our posture along the eastern flank, including with counter-drone ⁠capabilities. Nato will ​be sending ​additional assets ​to the region, ​including ‌support for surveillance, ​reconnaissance, ​and forensics.”

The deployment will include maritime patrol aircraft, radar systems, drones and intelligence personnel. There is mounting anxiety about the increasing overspill from Russia’s war on Ukraine and the potential for further friction with Nato.

Concern has been growing after alleged Russian attacks that have increasingly edged into the territorial waters and exclusive economic zones of Bulgaria and Romania. Romania deployed jets over the weekend to shoot down two suspected Russian drones over its territory.
Romania’s defence minister, Radu Miruță, said the drones were probably latest generation Russian drones, flying at speeds similar to fighter jets.

“The ones from last night were flying ​at 450 km/h, which leads us to think they were Russian-made Geran-4 drones with a turboprop ​engine,” Miruță said. “This is the first time we’ve shot down drones like these.”
Romania has recorded 35 unauthorised drone incursions so far this year, compared with nine in 2025. Romanian forces have downed six drones this year, compared with zero last year.

Last week, two chemical tankers were hit by drones near Romania’s Black Sea coast, the latest ​in a series of attacks that have highlighted the risks to commercial shipping on Nato’s eastern flank. Both vessels were anchored near ​the Sulina canal, which links the Danube River to the Black Sea and is an export route for Ukraine.

At least five other cargo ships have been hit near the coasts of Romania and Bulgaria in the ​past two weeks, with 23 sailors reported dead or missing. Most of those incidents ​occurred outside ⁠Nato territorial waters.
Amid mounting concern, Bulgaria has asked Nato for the deployment of combat aircraft and anti-drone systems to its territory. On 18 October, France sent a maritime reconnaissance aircraft to Romania.

The maritime insurer and risk analyst Ambrey has said there is no end in sight to the threats to Black Sea cargo shipping, including grain and oil, and that insurance prices for passage of the waters have rocketed.

Tomas Alexa, a senior analyst at Ambrey, said last week his company had noted a sharp increase in the tempo of attacks beginning in July. Russian forces are estimated to be responsible for 80% of them.

The recent loss of life, he suggested, had been exacerbated by “double tap” attacks involving aerial and surface drones, the latter often carrying up to half a tonne of explosive payloads. Smaller vessels that primarily use the Danube canal system have sunk rapidly.
“While attacks against merchant vessels in the Black Sea are not new, we are seeing an escalation both in terms of the number of attacks and in the geographical scope,” Alexa said.

articles.title: Like it or not, we have all benefited from the slave trade
articles.summary: Letter: Phil Hamlyn Williams responds to criticism of the Church of England’s plans for reparations
body: Thank you for the excellent research into the rightwing backlash against the Church of England’s proposals for reparations (Lobbying, lawyers and a media blitz: the fight to kill the Church of England’s £100m slavery compensation fund, 13 October). May I offer observations in two areas?

We are all beneficiaries of the slave trade, like it or not. The work that the Guardian is doing on the actions of its founders will enhance the historical record, but it is unlikely to change the broader picture identified by Eric Hobsbawm and others.

Cheap cotton picked by enslaved people fired the Industrial Revolution. Everything else flowed from it. The need for machinery demanded coal and iron. These begat steam engines, the railways, the factory system.

The benefits were not, and are not, evenly shared. My friend’s grandmother, who worked in a cotton mill at the age of 13, and so many like her suffered along with her brothers and sisters transported against their will from Africa.

Yet industrialisation transformed our lives. Take the example of cotton: the historian Roger Osborne offers a very telling statistic in his book Iron, Steam & Money: “In 1790, 4 per cent of clothing in Europe was made of cotton … by 1890, it had grown to 73 per cent while the European population had roughly doubled to 400 million.”

Industrialisation was not without its critics, not least John Ruskin. But its legacy is a world of disparity in wealth between and within nations, let alone the shadow of global warming. The evil of the slave trade lies at the heart of it. Individuals and families may have been responsible, but they are dead. It is with each of us in the postindustrial western world that discussion of reparations must start.
Let me turn now to the Church of England. While working for a C of E diocese, I struggled with hostile parishes refusing to pay their parish share. I can only imagine the current outcry.

May I suggest that it isn’t about reparations? These are people clinging to a disappearing world. Too few people are attending church to pay its way. As a bishop once said to me, these people have deep pockets, but very short arms. I suspect that pockets are no longer that deep.
Would it be wrong to repeat the oft-misquoted Bible passage from the letter to Timothy? The love of money is the root of all evil.Phil Hamlyn WilliamsOld Dalby, Leicestershire

articles.title: Parish churches need support to preserve the tradition of choral evensong
articles.summary: Letter: Dr Andrew James Sillett of St Giles’ church in Oxford says parish churches need help to flourish just as cathedrals do
body: Dr Coco Parkinson-Huggins (Letters, 13 October) is right to highlight the severe financial pressures facing England’s cathedrals and the threat that this poses to choral music. Yet the future of choral evensong depends not just on cathedrals. Across the country, there are parish churches that sustain choirs, train young organists and offer regular opportunities for children and adults to participate in this living tradition.

I am a churchwarden and singer at St Giles’ church in Oxford, where locally recruited choirs of boys, girls and teenagers sing choral evensong every Sunday. Alongside these choirs, around 40 organ students are currently learning through the church, and we are investing in a major new pipe organ to support future generations of musicians.

Parish churches often face many of the same financial pressures as cathedrals, but with fewer resources and less professional support. However, they remain uniquely placed to recruit locally and adapt quickly to changing circumstances.

At St Giles’ church, we are developing new ways of widening access to choral and organ education that should prove just as important to the future of the tradition as preserving historic institutions themselves.

If we focus only on preserving cathedrals, we risk overlooking the wider musical ecosystem that sustains English choral evensong. This tradition will flourish only if both cathedral and parish churches are enabled to pass it on to future generations.Dr Andrew James SillettChurchwarden, St Giles’ church, Oxford

articles.title: Why are French police so violent? Their job is to protect the state, not the people
articles.summary: Officers are instruments of state whose job is to repress, rather than manage, public dissent
body: Familiar images of teargas clouds drifting across Paris squares, police baton charges against masked protesters and terrified teenagers floored – and worse – by stun grenades have once again focused the world’s attention on France’s policing methods.

While most of its western European neighbours generally favour police tactics that prioritise crowd containment and de-escalation, France has long responded to social movements that take to the streets with, at times, shocking physical force.

The reasons why are a complex mix of history, politics, state organisation and a particular security culture that has become deeply ingrained over decades, if not centuries, and whose limits continue to be pushed today.

French policing policy is rooted in Napoleon’s ultra-centralised state and in the political philosophy of the Republic. In France, the police are an instrument of the state. Their core task is to protect it, enforce its laws, and maintain public order.

Conceptually, that is a far cry from, for example, the UK, where since the early 1800s the police have been considered servants of the public, whose authority derives from public consent and whose chief responsibility is to keep the peace.

French police officers are agents of state authority. That means protests, blockades and mass disorder are not just civil nuisances, but direct challenges to the authority of the republic. The police’s priority is to reclaim the streets, not to negotiate.

That explains the aggressive tactics, such as systematically encircling and trapping crowds, and the continued use of “intermediate” or less-than-lethal weapons, many of which are banned or heavily restricted elsewhere in Europe.

Defence ball launchers, for example, fire rubber projectiles at 185mph (300kph). The explosive grenades that injured gilets jaunes protesters in the late 2010s and killed an environmental protester in 2014 have been phased out, but been replaced by pyrotechnic stun grenades.

Designed to disperse crowds through both impact and a 160dB acoustic shock, these have caused multiple injuries in recent years, including lost eyes and teeth, fractured jaws and several amputated limbs. They also frequently instil mass panic.

Violent policing methods are also fostered by France’s almost unique culture of street protest. A legacy of insurrection dating back to the 1789 revolution means protesters know the street can, and generally does, force governments to back down.

Unlike in Germany or the Netherlands, French unions, while they may strike often, are not formal government negotiating partners. The top-heavy, presidential structure of the Fifth Republic also marginalises institutional consultation.

All that means a heavily centralised state may pass laws with little popular consent, making the “power of the street” one of citizens’ few viable means of winning concessions. Protest, here, is regarded as a civic duty and a legitimate democratic tool.

That creates a vicious circle. French authorities see large crowds as an existential threat, so send in the police. Their military-style tactics provoke even peaceful demonstrators, and prompt the more radical groups to violence.

And rather than trying to contain and isolate those elements, police respond with baton charges and munitions. The aggression is entrenched – and protests turn into piched battles between citizens and police.

Data from conflict monitoring organisations, such as Acled, consistently shows that France, perhaps surprisingly, does not always record western Europe’s highest number of demonstrations (Germany and Italy also vie for that title).

But it does show that France consistently records the highest rates of escalated, high-intensity unrest, including street barricades, widespread vandalism and looting, arson attacks and direct confrontations between protesters and police.

France’s approach to policing and crowd management has for decades drawn condemnation from international human rights monitors and civil society groups, including Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch and the Council of Europe.

Reports have documented instances of excessive force, misuse of grenades and rubber bullets, arbitrary mass arrests and routine teargas deployment against largely non-violent protesters. But the model persists, and is even expanding.

Last month, thousands marched in protest at a proposed “licence to kill” law seeking to establish a legal “presumption of self-defence” for police officers and gendarmes using firearms in the line of duty.

The law, opposed by civil rights groups, leftwing politicians, the magistrates’ union and the UN, would in effect shift the burden of proof on to victims and their families to demonstrate that a police shooting was disproportionate.

In essence, critics argue, it would institutionalise police impunity; reinforcing, once more, a security culture that treats public dissent and social tension not as democratic realities to be managed, but as insurrections to be repressed. The battle for France’s streets is far from over.

articles.title: Alberta voters overwhelmingly reject plan to leave Canada in referendum
articles.summary: Result is a victory for prime minister Mark Carney and supporters of Canadian unity
body: Voters in Canada’s Alberta have overwhelmingly rejected a proposal to begin the process of independence, delivering a decisive victory for supporters of Canadian unity and deepening divisions within the separatist movement.
With nearly 1.9m votes counted, roughly 76% people supported remaining in Canada, while 24% backed beginning a process toward separation, according to unofficial results from Elections Alberta.
The Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, who grew up in Edmonton, Alberta’s capital, celebrated the result.
“Albertans made a clear choice. They chose unity, to build together, and to take care of each other. Above all, Albertans chose Canada.”

He said the result would allow Canadians to move forward together and accelerate efforts to diversify trade, develop major infrastructure projects and make Canada a global energy powerhouse, with Alberta at its centre.
The results showed an overwhelming majority of Albertans had voted to remain and one radio show host posted: “Someone owes Albertans $130m for this theatrical waste of taxpayers’ money.”
Pollster David Coletto told the Guardian that residents felt the referendum was “a distraction away” from what they wanted their government to focus on.

“There was almost a general sadness about the wasted energy spent on this rather than the more real threats they see, including the Trump administration,” he said. “Most Albertans feel deep grievances with the federal government while also being proudly Canadian. The marriage may be rocky at times, and most Albertans want to see some thing changed, but very few are willing to see the marriage end.”

The province’s separatists, however, saw a silver lining. “We don’t have the final results. I think the numbers are going to fluctuate, but it is fair to say that at least a quarter of Albertans feel that Alberta needs to be treated better,” said Keith Wilson, a leader of the separatist movement.

Others took a different view of the results. “The result is bleak. Independence feels far away and we should not pretend this was not a defeat, however, it changes nothing about the reality of the circumstances Albertans find themselves in,” David Parker, a longtime far-right organiser linked to a massive breach of voter information, wrote on social media.

The Alberta premier, Danielle Smith, welcomed the early results, saying they showed widespread support for remaining in Canada. “Albertans have voted for a stronger Alberta in a united Canada,” Smith posted on social media.

Even though the vote was not explicitly about independence – a point that frustrated separatists – the ballot question nonetheless exposed divisions in Alberta’s politics and raised questions about the durability of national unity.

Delays at roughly 100 of the 1,400 at polling stations across the province pushed results back by more than two hours, but shortly after polls closed on Monday evening the results suggested a decisive win for those looking to remain in Canada.
Related: ‘This is not poker’: Alberta goes to polls in referendum that has exposed divisions, not least among separatists

The separation question – whether to remain in Canada or begin a legal process that could lead to a second vote – was one of 10 put to Albertans on Monday. The others covered issues including immigration, healthcare, education and the province’s constitutional powers. Elections Alberta said the remaining results could take days to count.
In the days leading up to the vote, provincial leaders and federal politicians crisscrossed the province to make the case for a unified country.

Carney warned against a vote from residents of the oil-rich province simply looking to “send a message” to the federal government. “A vote against Canada is a dangerous bluff that will lead to years of deep uncertainty and lost opportunities for Albertans and Canadians,” he told an energetic crowd last week.
The Conservative leader, Pierre Poilievre, whose parliamentary seat is in the province, told a crowd of supporters that Albertans were not “quitters”.

“To those people who are thinking about taking out their frustration on the current government by voting for separation in the referendum, I say this: Canada is more than a government,” he said. “It is a people, a flag, a land, a history and a promise.”

Data from Elections Alberta indicated roughly 43% of eligible voters – or 1.3 million Albertans – had already cast ballots before Monday’s vote through advance voting and mail-in ballots. That figure pointed to a potentially higher turnout than the province’s last referendum in 2021.

Smith’s tenure as leader of the United Conservative party is due in large part to separatists within the party who ousted her predecessor, Jason Kenney. In recent months she has tried to placate both the separatists and federalists in the party, in a province where a majority is not interested in secession.
The referendum became a political liability for Smith’s party, whose popular support has tumbled in recent months, including with the loss of a one-time conservative stronghold in a by-election.

Still, members of the separatist movement told the Guardian they would continue their push for independence. And in the aftermath of the results, one prominent separatist leader said he would push for a special general meeting of the party to remove Smith.

Jeffrey Rath told Global News that the Alberta independence will remain nothing but a dream long as Smith, whom he called an “avowed federalist” remains in power. He said it was time for separatists to “take back ownership” of the UCP.

In an interview before the results, the Calgary mayor, Jeromy Farkas, a staunch opponent of the independence movement, said the city’s “best future is here, as a Canadian city”, amid fears that uncertainty could lead to capital flight.

“I am Canadian because I’m Canadian, not in a transactional way and regardless of the flavour of prime minister,” Farkas said. “And I’m going to continue to make the case for how our future is strongest together, because no result will permanently put this to bed. “The separatist movement sees this as a long-term project.”
